"Good son! At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa prostrated himself before the Buddha Ratnagarbha with his head touching the ground. All sentient beings likewise attained this Samādhi of Non-deceit, obtained great benefit, gave rise to great compassion, and awakened the bodhicitta."
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa:
“With a noble mind, you have diligently arisen;
before me, for the sake of all sentient beings, you have well made a great vow.”
Able to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings,
causing their minds to be free from defilement; for this reason, in a future life,
they shall attain Buddhahood as the Honored One of devas and humans.

“Good son! At that time, having heard these verses, the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa was filled with great joy. He immediately rose, joined his palms, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Not far from the Buddha, he sat down again to listen to the Dharma.”
"At that time, the five hundred princes, including Prince Maśapava and the others, made this vow:
'May we obtain such variously adorned and meritorious buddha-fields, all exactly like the pure land cultivated by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganamudrā.'"

At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha bestowed upon each of them individually the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so that they would all simultaneously attain the Unsurpassed Way in other lands, just like the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganamudrā.
"Furthermore, the four hundred princes made this vow:
'We vow to take up a pure and wondrously adorned buddha-field, exactly like that of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrajñānaprabhāsa.'"

At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha likewise bestowed the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon each of them individually; they shall all simultaneously attain the Unsurpassed Way in different lands, just like the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrajñānaprabhāsa.
"Furthermore, eighty-nine princes also made this vow:
'We vow to take up such adorned Buddha-lands, equal and without distinction from those cultivated by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.'"
“At that time, eighty-four thousand minor kings each made distinct and extraordinary vows, and every one of them personally chose various kinds of adorned, most excellent Buddha-lands.”

At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha conferred upon each of them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, declaring that in a future age they would each, in different lands, simultaneously attain the Unsurpassed Way.
"At that time, twelve billion sentient beings also each made vows to attain various adorned and most excellent Buddha-lands.
Then, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha bestowed upon them all the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, saying:
'In a future age, in other lands, you shall all simultaneously realize the Unsurpassed Way.'"
“Good son! At that time, the brahmin Ratnasāgara had eighty sons, who were the brothers of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha; the eldest was named Sāgarabhuja.”
"Good son! At that time, the brahmacārin Ratnasāgara said to his eldest son:
'You should now take up a subtle, pure, and adorned buddha-field.'"
The son replied, "I only pray that the Venerable One will first deliver the lion's roar.
His father said to him:
"What I wish for shall be spoken last. His son spoke again:
"Does the wish I now make concern that which is pure or that which is impure?"
The father replied again:
"If there is a bodhisattva who has accomplished great compassion, only then will they take up an impure world. Why is this?"
“Because you wish to skillfully subdue the defilements of sentient beings, you should understand such matters for yourself. “Good son!
At that time, Sāgaradhara went to the place of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha and, standing before the Buddha, addressed the Buddha, saying:”
“World-Honored One!
I vow for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; when there are people with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, as in the world of the present Buddha, only then shall I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

I now further vow that all sentient beings within my land shall have their lust, anger, and delusion attenuated; that they shall feel weary of and seek detachment from body and mind, and become terrified of birth and death; that they shall perceive its faults and calamities, come to me to leave the household life and study the Way, and at that time, I shall preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for the sake of those sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha addressed Sāgarabuddhi, saying: "Good son!

In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed and you enter the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, there will be an eon named Ubhukāra-utpala-vyūha. This Buddha-world shall be named Praṇidhāna-priya. At that time, the lifespan of the people will be eighty thousand years; therein you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and your name shall be Ratnaparvata Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
At that time, Sāgarabuddhi again spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, may red pearls rain down all around this Jambūvana grove, and may all the trees spontaneously produce exquisite music.”

"Good son! At that time, Sāgarabuddhi bowed his head in prostration before the Buddha Ratnagarbha. At that very moment, red pearls rained down all around the garden, and from every tree there emerged various kinds of exquisite music."
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha spoke these verses for the young brahmin:
“Arise, O one of great power! You are an immeasurable treasury of wisdom.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you shall bring about great benefit.”
"My pure aspiration has now been fulfilled;
I shall become a teacher of gods and humans for the sake of all sentient beings. "Good son!

At that time, having heard these verses, Sāgarabuddhi was filled with great joy; he immediately rose, joined his palms, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Not far from the Buddha, he sat down again to listen to the Dharma.
"The second son of the brahmin, named Sambhava, addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
My present aspiration is like that of Sāgaradeva.'"
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha addressed Trapuṣa, saying:

"In a future age, during the Utpala Flower Kalpa, in the world called Praṇītarati, when the human lifespan has increased to eighty billion years, you shall therein attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and be named Sūryaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

"The world obtained by the third son shall likewise be such that, when the human lifespan is two thousand years, he will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, receiving the title Tathāgata Jvalanaghoṣarāja, up to Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One."
The fourth attained Buddhahood with the name Sumanas; the fifth attained Buddhahood with the name Śīlarāja; the sixth attained Buddhahood with the name Sudṛṣṭinetrin;
the seventh attained Buddhahood with the name Brahmavardhana; the eighth attained Buddhahood with the name Jambūchāyā;
the ninth attained Buddhahood with the name Pūrṇa; the tenth attained Buddhahood with the name...
In the eleventh [kalpa], he attained Buddhahood with the name Ratnagiri; in the twelfth, he attained Buddhahood with the name Sāgaragarbha;
in the thirteenth, he attained Buddhahood with the name Nārāyaṇa; in the fourteenth, he attained Buddhahood with the name Śikhin;
in the fifteenth, he attained Buddhahood with the name Namoni; in the sixteenth, he attained Buddhahood with the name Jñānottama; in the seventeenth, he attained...
In the nineteenth [kalpa], he became a Buddha named Kauṇḍinya; in the twentieth, a Buddha named Siṃhabala; in the twenty-first, a Buddha named Jñānadhvaja;
in the twenty-second, a Buddha named Ghoṣa; in the twenty-third, a Buddha named Uṣṇīṣavijaya;
in the twenty-fourth, a Buddha named Lokāntara-vinirgata; and in the twenty-fifth, a Buddha named Arthadarśin.
The twenty-fourth is the Buddha Jñānaprabha; the twenty-fifth is the Buddha Siṃhaguru;
the twenty-sixth is the Buddha Śāntajñāna; the twenty-seventh is the Buddha Nanda; the twenty-eighth is the Buddha Nyagrodharāja;
the twenty-ninth is the Buddha Suvarṇanetra; and the thirtieth is the Buddha Svayambhū.
Among the Buddhas, the thirty-first is named Sukhābha Buddha; the thirty-second, Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha;
the thirty-third, Sunetra Buddha; the thirty-fourth, Brahmakalyāṇarati Buddha;
the thirty-fifth, Brahmarṣi Buddha; the thirty-sixth, Brahmaghoṣa Buddha; and the thirty-seventh, Dharmacandra Buddha.
The thirty-eighth is named Buddha of Manifesting Meaning; the thirty-ninth is named Buddha of Joy; the fortieth is named Buddha of Increase;
the forty-first is named Buddha of Majestic Dignity; the forty-second is named Buddha of Exquisite Fragrance;
the forty-third is named Buddha of Supreme Vision; the forty-fourth is named Buddha of Skillful Contemplation; the forty-fifth is named...
The Buddha who embraces the meaning [of the Dharma], the forty-sixth being named Buddha of Noble Aspirations (Bhadra-praṇidhāna), the forty-seventh named Buddha of Supreme Wisdom (Jñānavara),
the forty-eighth named Buddha of the Golden Banner (Suvarṇadhvaja), the forty-ninth named Buddha of Excellent Eyes (Sunetra), the fiftieth named Buddha of Heavenly Radiance (Divyaprabha),
the fifty-first named Buddha of Pure Nourishment (Śuddhodana), and the fifty-second named Buddha of Good Vision (Sudarśana).
The fifty-third is named Vairocanaketu Buddha; the fifty-fourth is named Virūpākṣa Buddha;
the fifty-fifth is named Brahmaghoṣa Buddha; the fifty-sixth is named Guṇasaṃpanna Buddha;
the fifty-seventh is named Guṇaviśuddha Buddha; the fifty-eighth is named Ratnābhāsa Buddha; the fifty-ninth...
The ninth is named Maṇi-ratna Buddha; the sixtieth is named Śākyamuni Buddha; the sixty-first is named Ghoṣeśvararāja Buddha;
the sixty-second is named Jñānasaṃgata Buddha; the sixty-third is named Jayottama Buddha;
the sixty-fourth is named Puṣpasiddha Buddha; the sixty-fifth is named Supuṣpa Buddha; the sixtieth...
The sixth is named Buddha Without Anger; the sixty-seventh is named Buddha Sun-Treasury;
the sixty-eighth is named Buddha Honored Joy; the sixty-ninth is named Buddha Sun-Brightness; the seventieth is named Buddha Dragon-Attained;
the seventy-first is named Buddha Vajra-Light; the seventy-second is named Buddha Renowned King; the seventy-third is named Buddha Constant...
The Buddha Prabhāsa (Light-Radiance); seventy-fourth, the Buddha Lakṣaṇaprabhāsa (Mark-Radiance); seventy-fifth, the Buddha Śāṇiśūra;
seventy-sixth, the Buddha Jñānasiddha (Accomplishment of Wisdom); seventy-seventh, the Buddha Ghoṣarāja (King of Sound);
seventy-eighth, the Buddha Sālarājanārāyaṇagarbha (Sāla-King-Nārāyaṇa-Treasury); seventy-ninth, the Buddha Tejogarbha (Fire-Treasury).
“Good son! At that time, the youngest son of the brahmin, named Vigatabhayakleśa, stood before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
‘World-Honored One!’”

These seventy-nine persons have now been granted a prediction by the Buddha in his presence: during the Kalpa of the Universally Spread Utpala Flowers, in the world-system called Wish-Loved, when the lifespan of humans has increased further, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!

I now, before the Buddha, resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. In the latter part of the Utpala-flower kalpa, when I achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may my lifespan be exactly like the lifespans attained by the seventy-nine Buddhas;
and as for the sentient beings saved by those seventy-nine Buddhas, may the sentient beings I save be likewise.”
Just as the seventy-nine Buddhas taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, I likewise teach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles;
just as the number of śrāvaka disciples of those seventy-nine Buddhas was great or small, the number of my own disciples shall likewise be so.

Those immeasurable sentient beings whom those seventy-nine Buddhas were to transform during the Utpala Flower Kalpa—those who have received human bodies but have not yet attained liberation—I, having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this final kalpa, shall fully transform them all and cause them to abide in the Three Vehicles.
"Bhagavān! If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, I pray that the Bhagavān grant me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Good son! At that time, the Buddha Ratnagarbha praised Vigatabhayodvega, saying: 'Excellent!'"
Excellent! Son of good family,
you have now given rise to great compassion for immeasurable sentient beings.

"Good son! In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed and you enter the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, there will be an eon named Utpalā. During its latter portion, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and your name shall be Vimalapradīpanirgatarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The combined lifespans attained by these seventy-nine Buddhas total half a kalpa; your lifespan shall likewise be half a kalpa, and all that you previously vowed shall be fully accomplished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Free from Fear and Distress spoke again:
"World-Honored One!

If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, then as I now prostrate my head in reverence to the Buddha, may this world be rained upon on all sides with the subtle fragrance of *utpala* flowers. Should any sentient beings hear this fragrance, may the four great elements of their bodies become pure and free from defilement, becoming harmonious and well-adjusted, so that all their illnesses and sufferings are completely healed."
"Good son! At that time, after the Bodhisattva Free from Fear and Distress had spoken these words, he immediately prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet.

Thereupon, in this Buddha-world, a rain of exquisite *utpala* flowers and subtle fragrances fell everywhere. Any sentient beings who smelled them found the four great elements of their bodies purified and free from defilement; they became well-adjusted and harmonious, and all their sufferings of illness were completely healed."
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha spoke these verses for this bodhisattva:
"With a virtuous mind and compassion, O Guide, you may now arise;
All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, Unanimously praise you."
"Able to sever the firm and solid knots of all afflictions,
one shall in the future achieve goodness and become a treasury of pure wisdom. "Good son!"

At that time, having heard these verses, the Bodhisattva Free from Fear and Affliction was filled with great joy. He immediately rose, joined his palms, and went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet. Not far from the Buddha, he sat down again to listen to the Dharma.

“Good son! At that time, the brahmacārin Ratnasāgara had three hundred million disciples sitting together in one place outside the garden gate, teaching other sentient beings to take the three refuges and causing them to resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Good son! At that time, the brahmin exhorted his disciples, saying:
'You all should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and take up a buddha-field; you may now speak before the Buddha of whatever you seek according to your hearts' desires.'"
"Among these three hundred million people, there was one named Jyotiṣka who spoke thus:
'Venerable One! What is bodhi?'"
What are the factors that assist awakening?
How does a bodhisattva practice for awakening?
How does one attain awakening by binding the mind to mindfulness?
At that time, the teacher replied: “Māṇava!
Regarding what you have asked, ‘bodhi’ refers to the four inexhaustible treasuries (akṣaya-kośa) cultivated and accumulated by a bodhisattva.”
What are the four? They are:
the inexhaustible treasury of merit, the inexhaustible treasury of knowledge, the inexhaustible treasury of wisdom, and the inexhaustible treasury of the harmony of the Buddha-dharma.
"Noble son! This is called bodhi. Māṇava!"
As the Buddha has taught, the dharmas that assist awakening are what are called the methods for embracing the factors that aid purification and transcend birth and death.
Son of good family!
The relinquishing of wealth is itself a dharma that assists awakening, because it tames sentient beings.
Maintaining ethical discipline is a factor that aids the awakening of bodhi, for it brings about the fulfillment of one's vows;
patience is a factor that aids the awakening of bodhi, for it results in the perfection of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
diligence is a factor that aids the awakening of bodhi, for it brings all undertakings to completion.
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is a factor that aids awakening, for it brings the mind into a state of excellent subjugation;
wisdom (*prajñā*) is a factor that aids awakening, for it brings about the knowledge of all afflictions (*kleśa*);
extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) is a factor that aids awakening, for it results in the attainment of unimpeded eloquence (*apratihata-pratibhāna*).
Merit is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it is what all sentient beings require;
wisdom is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it brings about the accomplishment of unimpeded knowledge;
tranquility is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it brings about the accomplishment of a supple and virtuous mind.
Contemplation is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it accomplishes the severance of doubt;
a mind of loving-kindness is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it accomplishes an unobstructed mind;
a mind of compassion is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it brings about the teaching and transformation of sentient beings without weariness.
A mind of joy is an aid to the factors of enlightenment, for it engenders love and delight for the True Dharma;
a mind of equanimity is an aid to the factors of enlightenment, for it accomplishes the severance of the states of attachment and aversion;
listening to the Dharma is an aid to the factors of enlightenment, for it accomplishes the destruction of the five hindrances.
Transcending the world is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it accomplishes the relinquishing of all worldly things;
forest hermitages are factors conducive to enlightenment, for they cause unwholesome deeds to be extinguished so they do not arise, and cause all roots of goodness to increase greatly;
mindfulness is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it accomplishes protective maintenance.
Volition is a factor conducive to enlightenment, because it accomplishes the discernment of all phenomena;
mindfulness is a factor conducive to enlightenment, because it accomplishes the awakening through reflection;
the foundations of mindfulness are factors conducive to enlightenment, because they accomplish the discernment of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Right effort is a factor conducive to enlightenment, because it abandons all unwholesome dharmas and cultivates and expands all wholesome dharmas;
the bases of psychic power are factors conducive to enlightenment, because they accomplish lightness and agility of body and mind;
the faculties are factors conducive to enlightenment, because they encompass and perfect the faculties.
The various powers (*bala*) are factors that assist awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), for they crush and destroy all afflictions (*kleśa*);
awakening (*bodhi*) is a factor that assists awakening, for it realizes the true Dharma;
and the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) are factors that assist awakening, for they subdue sentient beings and cause them to become pure.
“Māṇava! This is called the Dharma-gate of embracing the factors that assist in purifying the crossing over of birth and death.
Jyotiṣka spoke again:
"Venerable One!

As the Buddha has taught: the fruit of giving is great wealth and the acquisition of a large retinue; upholding the precepts leads to rebirth in the heavens; and extensive learning results in the attainment of great wisdom."
"Furthermore, as the Buddha has said, by means of the method of contemplation, one attains liberation from birth and death.
The teacher replied again: "Māṇava!"
If one practices giving because one delights in birth and death, for that reason one becomes very wealthy. O Māṇava!
If a son or daughter of good family directs their mind toward bodhi and practices giving in order to tame the mind;
One upholds the precepts for the sake of mental tranquility;
one seeks extensive learning for the sake of mental purity and freedom from the turbidity of craving;
and one contemplates the cultivation of the path for the sake of great compassion.
As for all other dharmas, they assist in the pursuit through the accomplishment of wisdom and skillful means.
Māṇava! These are called the factors that assist awakening.
To practice in this way is precisely to attain bodhi by binding the mindfulness. Māṇava!
Thus, one should now generate the desire for bodhi; this path is pure, and one should cultivate the vow with single-minded devotion.
This path is free from turbidity because the mind is pure;
this path is upright and without guile because it severs the afflictions;
this path is peaceful and secure because it can lead all the way to the city of Nirvana.
"You all should now make great and virtuous vows to take up the adornment of Buddha-lands, according to whatever purity or impurity you desire.
"O sons of good family!"
At that time, the young brahmin Jyotiṣka knelt with his right knee on the ground before the Buddha Ratnagarbha, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

I now resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. When all sentient beings in this impure world have little greed, anger, or delusion; when they do not transgress the Dharma, their minds are free from the turbidity of craving and thoughts of enmity or malice; when they abandon stinginess and envy, leave behind wrong views and abide in right view, and depart from unwholesome states of mind to seek all wholesome dharmas; when they leave behind the three evil minds to seek the three good paths, accomplish roots of goodness within the three bases of merit, and diligently cultivate and accumulate the practices of the Three Vehicles—at that time, I shall realize the Unsurpassed Way.
“World-Honored One!
If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, may two white dragon-elephants spontaneously emerge from my two hands.

Having spoken these words, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, two dragon-elephants immediately emerged from his hands; they were pure white in color, with seven parts of their bodies touching the ground.
"Having seen this, he said: 'Nāgas and elephants!

You should now go to the sky not far from here and rain down everywhere throughout this realm the perfumed water of the eight virtues. Awaken all sentient beings in this realm; if any sentient beings encounter even a single drop or smell its fragrance, they shall all sever the five hindrances—namely, the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.'"

Having spoken these words, at that time the two dragon-elephants moved swiftly through the air, circling like a strong man releasing a well-aimed arrow. Once they had completed all their tasks, they returned once more and stood before the māṇava.
At that time, having witnessed these events, Jyotiṣka was filled with great joy.
"O son of good family!
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha addressed the young brahmin (māṇava) as follows:"

“Good son! In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed, upon entering the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, there will be an eon named Sound-Light (Ghoṣaprabha). At that time, this Buddha-world shall be renamed Harmonious Sound-Light (Saṃghoṣaprabha). Therein you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and your title shall be Ratnacchatravardhamānaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
“Good son! At that time, Druma prostrated himself with his head to the ground, paying homage at the feet of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha then spoke these verses for Druma:”
"His mind is free from defilement, pure and awakened;
now he has received the prophecy, and is able to cause immeasurable billions of sentient beings to purify the supreme path."
"In a future age, you shall be a Tamer of Gods and Humans.

"Good son! At that time, having heard these verses, Śruti was filled with great joy; he immediately rose, joined his palms, and went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet. Not far from the Buddha, he sat down again to listen to the Dharma."
Of the three hundred million disciples, with the exception of one thousand people, all the rest made a vow with one voice to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this world.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha bestowed the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon each and every one of them.
This continued until Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū, who finally attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"The remaining thousand people all recited the Vedic scriptures. Among them, the one most highly revered was named Vyāsa, who addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"

My present vow is that I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this world of five turbidities, and for the sake of these sentient beings who are burdened with heavy greed, hatred, and delusion, and afflicted by much distress, I shall preach the True Dharma.
At that time, among the thousand people, there was another man named Agniskandha who spoke these words:
"Venerable Pāyāsi! For what purpose have you seen it fit to vow to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within this world of five corruptions?"
The teacher replied:
"Because this bodhisattva has accomplished great compassion, he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in an age of five turbidities."

At that time, sentient beings have no protector or refuge, and they lack virtuous thoughts; their minds are constantly disturbed by afflictions and invaded by various views. It is within such a world that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thereby able to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, skillfully acting as their protection, providing them with a dwelling, a shelter, and a lamp of light. Furthermore, one delivers them from the great ocean of birth and death, instructing them to abide in right view, leading them to dwell in nirvāṇa and drink the water of ambrosia. Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to manifest great compassion, he vows to take birth in such a world of the five turbidities.
"Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha addressed Pāyubandhu, saying: 'Good son!'"

In a future age, after the passing of one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges River, during the latter part of a second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges River, there will be a world named Kāṣāyadhvaja, located to the east of this buddha-world at a distance equal to the number of atoms in a buddha-field. Therein, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and your name shall be Suvarṇaparvatarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, Pāyubhiñju again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, I now prostrate my head at the Buddha’s feet; I only pray that the Tathāgata will place his two feet, adorned with the hundred merits, upon the crown of my head.”
“Good son! At that time, after Pāyāsinī had spoken these words, he immediately paid homage at the feet of the Buddha Ratnagarbha.
Instantly, the Tathāgata’s feet—endowed with the merit of a hundred blessings—rested upon his head, and the Buddha further praised him with this verse:”
“O you of great compassionate heart, may you now arise once more;
with wisdom sharp and keen, practice the bodhisattva path for the sake of awakening, and sever the firm bonds.”
"Though bound by all afflictions, he shall attain Buddhahood in the future and be able to bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings. "Good son!"

At that time, having heard these verses, Pāyāsi was filled with great joy; he immediately rose, joined his palms, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Not far from the Buddha, he sat down again to listen to the Dharma.
“Good son! At that time, the young brahmin Agniskandha knelt with his right knee on the ground before the Buddha Ratnagarbha, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

‘The vow I now make is to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this world. If there are sentient beings whose three poisons are equal in measure, who cannot dwell single-mindedly in wholesome dharmas, whose minds are not virtuous, and whose lifespan is forty thousand years—at that time, I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha addressed Jvālāmālin, saying: "Good son!

In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed, during the latter part of a second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, this buddha-world shall be named Sahā."
For what reason is it called Sahā?
Because the sentient beings therein endure the three poisons and all afflictions, that realm is therefore named the Land of Endurance (Sahā).
At that time, there was a great eon named Bhadra.
For what reason was this eon called Bhadra?

Because within this great eon, although there were many sentient beings possessed of greed, anger, ignorance, and pride, there appeared in the world one thousand World-Honored Ones who had perfected great compassion.

"Good son! At the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was forty thousand years, he was the very first among the thousand Buddhas to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. He was named Krakucchanda Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. For the sake of all sentient beings, he preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, causing immeasurable beings who were caught in birth and death to all attain liberation and abide in Nirvāṇa."
“Good son! At that time, the young brahmin Agniveśya prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to one side, and sat down again to listen to the Dharma. Good son!”
At that time, the second māṇava, whose name was Ākāśa, sat before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In a future age, following after the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, when the human lifespan is thirty thousand years, I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Gaganagañja, saying: “Good son!

In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed, and during the latter part of a second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, within the Bhadrakalpa, in the Sahā world, following the Buddha Krakucchanda when the human lifespan is thirty thousand years, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi therein. You shall be named Kanakamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; your great fame shall be heard throughout the world.”

At that time, having heard his prediction of enlightenment, Ākāśa prostrated himself before the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood before him. Scattering various kinds of flowers over the Buddha’s body, he joined his palms in reverent salutation and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“Guarding and protecting body and mind, He skillfully enters meditative concentration;
With subtle and wondrous voice, He is well able to provide instruction and admonition.”
His mind is pure and free from turbidity or confusion;
though he transforms sentient beings, he does not violate worldly dharmas.
His fame is radiant, and he possesses mindfulness and dhāraṇī.
The merit of a hundred blessings increases and expands without exception;
for the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests the path of goodness,
raises the supreme banner of the immortals, and accumulates a mountain of merit.
Sustaining and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings,
causing them all to be fully perfected in merit;
furthermore, bestowing upon sentient beings the path of sublime quiescence.
The afflictions he burns away are like Mount Sumeru;
within the three realms of existence, he gives rise to great compassion and bestows predictions of enlightenment upon immeasurable sentient beings.

“Good son! At that time, the third young brahmin, whose name was Viśākha, stood before the Buddha and made an offering to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus using a bed of the seven precious gems. Upon this bed were spread carpets and cushions worth ten million taels of gold; upon the bed he placed a vessel of pure gold filled with the seven precious gems, along with a pure gold water pitcher and a wondrous staff of the seven precious gems.”
Having made this offering, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, and during the latter part of a second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, may I enter the Bhadrakalpa and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

At that time, the lifespan of human beings will have diminished, and they will have entered the first stage of the five turbidities. All sentient beings will possess thick and heavy greed, lust, anger, delusion, stinginess, and jealousy; they will practice false views, follow evil associates, and their minds will be shrouded by various unwholesome roots. Their hearts will sink and retreat from all wholesome roots; they will distance themselves from right view and sustain themselves through wrong livelihoods.

After the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa-muni and the extinction of the True Dharma, when all sentient beings are blind and lack the eye of wisdom, having no teacher or lineage to follow, and the human lifespan is twenty thousand years—at that time, I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha praised Viśākunta, saying: ‘Excellent!’”
Excellent! Son of good family,
you have now accomplished unsurpassed wisdom.

"When you first entered the five turbidities of this evil world, the lifespan of people was twenty thousand years; they were blind, lacking the eye of wisdom, and had no teacher or lineage to follow. Within such conditions, you attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; now, your name shall be Great Compassionate Wisdom."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika-jñāna: “Good son!

In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed, and during the latter part of a second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, you will enter the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan is twenty thousand years. At that time, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and your name shall be Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

"Good son! At that time, the Bodhisattva Great Compassionate Wisdom immediately prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and made offerings to the World-Honored One with various flowers, powdered incense, and unguents. He then praised the Buddha in verse:
‘O Honored One among Men, Benefactor of sentient beings,
They are able to cause all those beings to give rise to a heart of love and joy;
through the dharma-gate of mindfulness and concentration, their minds attain single-mindedness.
Hearing this wondrous sound, my heart is filled with great joy.
With wisdom and skillful means fully perfected,
he is thus able to practice the teaching and transformation of the world.
Furthermore, together with immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, he...
They are granted the prediction of the path to unsurpassed bodhi;
by this cause, they are able to behold the Buddhas of the ten directions,
whose wisdom and supernormal powers are entirely equal.
All the subtle and wondrous merits possessed by all Buddhas,
as well as their manifestations, their cultivation of the bodhisattva path,
and their conferring of the prediction of supreme enlightenment upon all sentient beings.
"If one wished to praise them, it could not be exhausted;
therefore, I now bow my head in reverent salutation.
At that time, the Brahmin Ratnasāgara again addressed the fourth māṇava, Viśaya-vimala, saying:
“Good son! You should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. “Good son! [he said].
At that time, Viśayā-vimala stood before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I vow to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within this world during the Bhadrakalpa, and not amidst the five turbidities of an evil age such as the land of Kāśyapa Buddha."

After the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and the extinction of the True Dharma, the lifespan of humans will decrease further until it reaches ten thousand years. All acts of giving, self-discipline, and observance of the precepts will completely perish; the wholesome minds of these sentient beings will gradually vanish, and they will become estranged from the seven riches. They will regard evil associates as World-Honored Ones, never develop a mind for training in the three meritorious activities, abandon the three virtuous conducts, and diligently practice the three evils. With their wisdom-minds shrouded by various afflictions, they will be rendered sightless and have no desire to study or train in the Three Vehicles.

Among these sentient beings, if I were to seek to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there would be no one at all capable of creating an obstacle; how much less so when the human lifespan is one thousand years!
Until the human lifespan reaches one hundred years, at that time sentient beings will not even have the names of wholesome dharmas, let alone those who practice roots of goodness.

In this world of five turbidities, as the lifespans of people gradually diminish until they reach ten years and the kalpa of swords arises again, I shall descend from the heavens at that time to protect sentient beings. I will manifest wholesome dharmas for them, causing them to leave unwholesome dharmas behind, and lead them to abide securely within the ten wholesome paths of action. Freeing them from the afflictions and fetters of the ten unwholesome actions, I shall cause them all to be completely purified. Having extinguished the beings of the world of five turbidities, until the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years, at that time I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, sentient beings will have little greed, anger, delusion, ignorance, stinginess, or envy; at that time, I shall preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for all these sentient beings, enabling them to dwell in peace and stability.
“World-Honored One!
If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, I pray that the Tathāgata will grant me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

"Bhagavān! If I were not to receive such a prediction of enlightenment, I would now seek the vehicle of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; by the power of whichever vehicle I had adopted, I would swiftly attain liberation and cross over from birth and death."
Then the Buddha Ratnagarbha said to Viśayāmala: "Good son! There are four kinds of indolence for a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will become attached to birth and death, undergo various sufferings within the prison of birth and death, and will not be able to quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
What are the four?
Inferior conduct, inferior companions, inferior giving, and inferior aspirations.
What is the bodhisattva’s inferior conduct?
There may be a bodhisattva who violates the precepts of body and speech and cannot guard them well; this is called "inferior conduct.
What is meant by "inferior companions"? To associate with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and engage in their affairs together—this is called the "inferior companions" of a bodhisattva.
What is meant by "inferior giving"?

When one cannot relinquish all that one possesses, but instead gives rise to discriminatory thoughts toward the recipients, practicing generosity for the sake of attaining pleasure in the heavens, this is called the Bodhisattva’s inferior giving (*hīna-dāna*).
What is inferior aspiration (*hīna-praṇidhāna*)?

To be unable to single-mindedly aspire to take up the pure and wondrous worlds of all Buddhas, and to make vows that do not aim to subdue and transform all sentient beings—this is called the inferior vow of a bodhisattva.

When a bodhisattva establishes these four factors of indolence, they will dwell for a long time in saṃsāra, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, and will be unable to swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are four dharmas which, when accomplished by a bodhisattva, enable them to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are the four?
First, being able to uphold the prohibitive precepts, purifying body, speech, and mind, and guarding the practice of the Dharma;
second, drawing near to and studying under those who practice the Mahāyāna, sharing the same purpose as the Dharma.
Third, one is able to relinquish all possessions, bestowing them upon all beings with a mind of great compassion;
fourth, one single-mindedly vows to take up various adorned Buddha-worlds, also for the sake of taming and transforming all sentient beings.
These are called the four dharmas that a bodhisattva accomplishes, whereby they can swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas that a bodhisattva accomplishes, which enable them to uphold the path to unsurpassed bodhi."
What are the four?
Diligently practicing all the pāramitās;
gathering in all immeasurable sentient beings;
The mind is never apart from the practice of the four immeasurables;
one sports with the various supernormal powers.
These are called the four dharmas which, when accomplished by a bodhisattva, enable them to uphold the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas that cause the mind to never grow weary. What are these four?
First, practicing giving; second, listening to the Dharma; third, cultivating practice; and fourth, gathering in sentient beings.”
"These four dharmas cause the mind to never grow weary; a bodhisattva should train in them.
Furthermore, there are four inexhaustible treasuries that all bodhisattvas should accomplish."
What are the four?
First, the faculty of faith; second, the teaching of the Dharma; third, the aspiration for roots of goodness; and fourth, the gathering in of impoverished sentient beings.
These are the four inexhaustible treasuries that a bodhisattva fully cultivates and perfects.
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas of purity that a bodhisattva accomplishes.
What are the four?
Purity of ethical discipline through the absence of self;”
Samādhi is pure because there are no sentient beings;
wisdom is pure because there is no life-principle;
and the knowledge and vision of liberation is pure because there is no person.

These are the four dharmas of purity; because Bodhisattvas accomplish them, they swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the wheel of Dharma that is like space, the inconceivable wheel of Dharma, the immeasurable wheel of Dharma, the wheel of non-self, the wheel of ineffability, the supramundane wheel of Dharma, the wheel of thorough penetration, and the subtle and wondrous wheel that neither gods nor humans can turn.

“Good son! In a future age, after one *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed, and during the latter part of a second *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, at the very beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, once the five corruptions have been extinguished and the lifespan has increased to eighty thousand years, you shall therein attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and be named Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

At that time, the young Brahmin Viśākha stood before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. He then made offerings of various flowers, powdered incense, and unguents to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, praising the Buddha in verse:
“The World-Honored One is stainless, Like a mountain of pure gold;
The tuft of hair between his brows Is as white as jade or snow.”
At that time, for my sake, you preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
you prophesied that in a future age I would become a Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Who, having seen or heard this, would not accept it?
"The sages, the great awakened ones, the lamps of the world—what are their merits? "Good son!

At that time, among the thousand young brahmins of the brahmin-rishi Ratnasāgara, with the exception of one person, they all recited the Vedas and external scriptures; yet they had all been exhorted toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just like Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Maitreya."
The fifth was named Siṃhaprabha, and it was likewise.

Among those thousand people, with the exception of one individual, all the others vowed to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the Bhadrakalpa. The lowest and most junior among that assembly was named Vegadhārī; the brahmacārin Ratnasāgara further instructed him to resolve his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"Do not look back to the distant past; you should abandon mental perceptions and give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
At that time, the brahmin, possessing swift and powerful faculties, spoke these verses:
"The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases— the sentient beings encompassed by them..."
Dreading old age, sickness, and death, they fall into the ocean of craving and are confined within the three realms of existence,
in a terrifying prison where they drink the poison of afflictions and mutually inflict harm upon one another.
For a long night they have fallen into the sea of suffering and affliction;
blind and sightless through ignorance, they have lost the right path and long dwelt within birth and death, shrouded by the machinery of conditioned existence.
Sentient beings within the three realms of existence are ablaze with all manner of suffering.
Because they have abandoned right view and dwell securely in false views,
they wander through birth and death amidst the five destinies.
They find no rest, like the wheels of a chariot.
There are sentient beings who have lost the eye of Dharma;
blind and seeing nothing, they are without protection or refuge.
You should cultivate and accumulate immeasurable wisdom to free yourself from delusion;
cause the aspiration for enlightenment to arise,
and act as a virtuous friend to all sentient beings.
To burn away the fetters of craving and untie the bonds of affliction,
one should, for the sake of such beings, resolve upon the bodhicitta.
Those who have lost the eye of Dharma are shrouded by delusion.
To bring about freedom from delusion, one should bestow the supreme path;
for the prison of birth and death is ablaze with great fires,
and one must provide the nectar of the Dharma to satisfy them completely.
Go now with haste to where the Buddha is;
prostrate yourself at his feet and bring about great benefit.
At the presence of the Buddha, you should make a sublime and supreme vow.
May your sublime aspirations be well-maintained in mind.
In future ages, you shall become a Tamer of gods and humans;
you should likewise vow to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
Rescuing all beings, you cause them all to be liberated;
you also cause them to be fully endowed with the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment.
You rain down the great Dharma rain and bestow the water of wisdom.
"Extinguish the fires of suffering and affliction for all sentient beings. "Good son!
At that time, the one named Swift Power (Dhṛtibalajava) spoke these words:"
“Venerable One!
As for my present aspiration, I do not seek the retribution of birth and death, nor do I seek the vehicle of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha;

I now seek only the unsurpassed Mahāyāna. I await the proper time and place, I await the taming of sentient beings, and I await the arousal of virtuous vows; it is these matters that I am currently contemplating.”
"Venerable One!
Wait but a moment and hear my lion’s roar.
At that time, O son of good family!

At that time, the Brahmā-ascetic Ratnasāgara gradually retreated, accompanied by five attendants: the first named Hastināga, the second named Sthalanāga, the third named Jalenāga, the fourth named Ākāśanāga, and the fifth named Svaranāga.
He addressed them, saying: "You all should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The five men replied, "Venerable One!
We are destitute and possess nothing with which to make offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks."
"Having not yet planted roots of goodness, how can one give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? "Good son!

At that time, the brahmin took the jeweled earring from his left ear and gave it to the Dragon of the Hand; he took the jeweled earring from his right ear and gave it to the Dragon of the Land; he took the jeweled couch upon which he sat and gave it to the Dragon of the Water; he gave the jeweled staff he used to the Dragon of Space; and he gave the pure gold water-pitcher to the Dragon of Wondrous Sound."
Having given it to him in this way, he spoke again: "Young man!
You should now take these items to make offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks, and resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Sutra of the Compassionate Flower, Scroll Five;
The Sutra of the Compassionate Flower, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Original Prophecy of the Bodhisattvas, Part Four.
At that time, the five men went to where the Buddha was and offered the goods they had obtained to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
Having made these offerings, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Tathāgata will grant me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so that I may attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within this Bhadrakalpa."
“Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha immediately bestowed upon those five people the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, saying:
‘Hand Dragon!...’”
"In a future age, during the Bhadrakalpa, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Tathāgata Dṛḍhasvara, fully endowed with the ten titles.
After the parinirvāṇa of Tathāgata Dṛḍhasvara, Lusheng (Sthalanāga) shall next become a Buddha, named Tathāgata Sukhadeva, fully endowed with the ten titles."
After the Buddha Sukhāvatīrāja attains parinirvāṇa, the Water Dragon shall next attain Buddhahood, named the Tathāgata Śāstṛ, endowed with the ten titles.
After the Buddha Śāstṛ attains parinirvāṇa, the Ākāśa Dragon shall next attain Buddhahood, named the Tathāgata Priyaviśuddha, endowed with the ten titles.
After the Buddha Pure Love attains parinirvāṇa, the Dragon Fine Sound shall next become a Buddha, named Nārāyaṇavijayapatra Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles.

“Good son! After the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha had bestowed prophecies upon these five men that they would attain Buddhahood in the Bhadrakalpa, the brahmacārin Ratnasāgara again addressed Dhāraṇīśvaravega: ‘Good son!’”

You may now take up various kinds of pure and wondrous worlds for adornment according to what your heart delights in, and you may then make a vow to bestow the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma upon all sentient beings. With single-minded diligence, practice the Bodhisattva path, and be careful not to dwell on the vastness of the kalpas.
"Good son! At that time, the brahmin took hold of the arm of Balavegavat and led him to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha's presence, he sat before the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:"
“World-Honored One!
In future ages, within this Bhadrakalpa, how many Buddha-suns, Tathāgatas, will appear in the world?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Dhāraṇīśvaravega, saying:
“Good son! During the half-aeon of the Bhadra-kalpa, one thousand four Buddhas will appear in the world. Dhāraṇī-vega said:
“World-Honored One!

After all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of that Bhadrakalpa have entered parinirvāṇa, the last one, Suparṇa the Nāga, shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and his name shall be Narayana-vijaya-patra.”
"World-Honored One!

I vow that at that time I shall cultivate the bodhisattva path and practice various ascetic disciplines, fully perfecting all manner of aids to the path—observing the precepts, practicing generosity, extensive learning, diligence, patience, kind speech, merit, and wisdom."

"When the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa are about to attain Buddhahood, may I be the first to offer them food and drink; after their parinirvāṇa, may I collect their relics and erect stupas to make offerings to them."
They uphold the True Dharma; seeing those who violate the precepts, they exhort and transform them, establishing them so that they abide in the observance of the precepts;
seeing those who have fallen away from right view into various false views, they exhort and transform them, establishing them so that they abide in right view;
and for those with distracted minds, they exhort and transform them, establishing them so that they abide in a concentrated mind.
For those who lack dignified deportment, I shall exhort and settle them so that they abide in noble deportment.
If there are sentient beings who wish to practice roots of goodness, I shall reveal and explain those roots of goodness for them.

After those World-Honored Ones have entered parinirvāṇa and when the True Dharma is on the verge of extinction, I shall at that time protect and uphold it so that it is not severed, and I shall kindle the lamp of the True Dharma within the world.

During the kalpa of weapons, I shall teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them to uphold the precept against killing up to right view. From among the ten unwholesome paths of action, I shall pull sentient beings out and establish them securely within the ten wholesome paths of action, extinguishing all blindness and darkness, and revealing the wholesome dharmas.
I shall extinguish these five corruptions—corruption of the eon, corruption of lifespan, corruption of sentient beings, corruption of afflictions, and corruption of views—leaving none remaining.

During the eon of famine, I shall exhort and transform all sentient beings, establishing them securely in the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), and likewise for the perfections up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
When I exhort sentient beings to abide in the six pāramitās, I cause all their hunger, darkness, defilement, hostile robbers, strife, and various afflictions to be completely stilled.

During the kalpa of pestilence, I shall teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them all to abide in the six dharmas of harmony and likewise to dwell securely in the four methods of attraction; I shall cause all the pestilences and darknesses of sentient beings to be completely extinguished.
During the latter half of this Bhadrakalpa, I shall eradicate such sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings.
After one thousand four Buddhas have appeared in the world during this half-kalpa, entered parinirvāṇa, and their True Dharma has vanished, I shall then attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Just as the lifespan and śrāvaka disciples attained by the fourteen thousand Buddhas, so too shall my lifespan and śrāvaka disciples be equal to theirs, without any distinction.
Just as the fourteen thousand Buddhas subdued sentient beings during half an eon, I vow that I too shall subdue sentient beings during half of this Bhadrakalpa.

During this half-eon, may there be no śrāvaka disciples of the various Buddhas who violate the prohibitions and precepts, fall into various views, lack reverence toward the Buddhas, give rise to thoughts of anger and malice, disrupt the Dharma and destroy the Sangha, slander the worthy and holy ones, ruin the True Dharma, or commit acts of parricide and other heinous crimes.
"Bhagavān! When I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall pull all beings out from the mire of birth and death and cause them to enter the city of fearless nirvāṇa."
After my parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma and the Bhadrakalpa shall both perish at once.

When my nirvāṇa has occurred and both the True Dharma and the Bhadrakalpa have been extinguished, my teeth, bones, and śarīra relics shall all undergo transformation to become images of Buddhas. Their bodies shall be adorned with the thirty-two marks, and within each mark there shall be the eighty secondary characteristics, arranged in successive order as ornaments. These shall pervade the infinite, boundless worlds throughout the ten directions where no Buddha currently dwells; each transformed Buddha shall teach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to infinite, boundless sentient beings, causing them all never to regress.
If, in that world, a kalpa of illness arises and there is no Buddha-dharma, these emanated Buddha-images shall likewise go there and teach and transform sentient beings as previously described.
If there are worlds that lack precious jewels, may I become a wish-fulfilling maṇi gem, raining down all manner of treasures and causing natural stores of pure gold to emerge.

If there are sentient beings in all worlds who are devoid of roots of goodness and whose bodies are entangled in various sufferings, I shall, within those realms, rain down uśīra incense, sandalwood, aloeswood, and various other fragrances, causing all sentient beings to sever the disease of afflictions, the disease of false views, and the diseases of the four great elements of the body; and by diligently practicing with a devoted mind in the three bases of merit, may they, at the time of death, be reborn among gods and humans.
"Bhagavān! When I practice the bodhisattva path, I shall bring benefit to sentient beings in this way.
Once I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall perform the buddha-work in this way."
"After my parinirvāṇa, my relics shall further reach immeasurable worlds, thus benefiting sentient beings in this way.
"World-Honored One!

If my vow is not fulfilled and I do not attain my own benefit, if I cannot act as a Great Physician-King for all sentient beings and bring them benefit, then I would now be deceiving the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, currently residing in every place throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions; furthermore, they should not have bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Among the immeasurable, boundless billions of *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings for whom the World-Honored One has bestowed the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I have not seen such people as these, nor have I heard the voice of the Buddha, the sounds of the Dharma and the Saṅgha, or the sound of practicing wholesome dharmas; I have constantly fallen into the Avīci Hell."
“World-Honored One!
If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, may the Tathāgata now praise me.
At that time, the Buddha immediately praised Dhāraṇīśvararāja:
"Excellent! Excellent!
Well-spoken, son of good family!"

"In a future age, you shall become a Great King of Physicians, causing all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction; therefore, I name you Vaidūryaprabhāśvararāja (Fire-Pure Medicine King).
The Buddha said to Vaidūryaprabhāśvararāja:

"In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa as numerous as the sands of the Ganges has passed, during the latter part of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, within the Bhadrakalpa when the one thousand four Buddhas are on the verge of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, you shall be able to offer them food and drink, and everything else up to that which you have previously vowed."

After the parinirvāṇa of Narayana-vijaya and the extinction of his True Dharma, you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, known by the name Loushi Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, Vidya-carana-sampanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Purusa-damya-sarathi, Sasta-deva-manusyanam, Buddha, Bhagavan. Your lifespan shall be half a kalpa; the number of Sravaka disciples you shall obtain will be equal and indistinguishable from those of the fourteen thousand Buddhas.

After you have converted sentient beings, following your parinirvana and the extinction of the True Dharma, when the Bhadrakalpa has come to an end, your teeth and bone relics shall all transform into Buddhas, and even those born among devas and humans shall likewise do so.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Agnidatta Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, I pray only that the Tathāgata will, with his golden hand adorned with the hundred merits, stroke the crown of my head."
"Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha took his hand, adorned with the merit of a hundred blessings, and stroked the crown of Jvalanaprabha Bhaiṣajyarāja’s head. Good son!"

At that time, the Bodhisattva Agnidatta Bhaiṣajyarāja, having witnessed these events, felt great joy in his heart; he immediately prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Brahmā-volunteer Ratnasāgara gave a celestial, exquisite robe to the Bodhisattva Agnidatta-rājaputra and praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son! Your aspiration is most extraordinary and sublime.
From this day forward, you shall no longer need to serve me as my attendant; you shall always be able to practice the 'Conduct of Peaceful Bliss' with complete autonomy."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
“Good son! At that time, the brahmacārin Ratnasāgara thought to himself:”
"I have now exhorted immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings, causing them to abide in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
I now see that these great bodhisattvas have each made vows to take up pure buddha-fields, with the sole exception of one person, Vyūhavīṇu.

Among the other bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa, they too shall be free from the five corruptions. I, however, shall now, within this final age, provide the flavor of the true Dharma to all sentient beings; I shall now personally fortify my adornments and make various virtuous vows, like the roar of a lion, so that when all the bodhisattvas hear them, their hearts will be filled with wonder and they will exclaim at such an unprecedented marvel.

Furthermore, may the entire great assembly—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—join their palms in reverence and pay homage to me; may the Buddha, the World-Honored One, praise me and grant me a prophecy; and may the present Buddhas throughout the ten directions, infinite and boundless, in every place, preach the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

When those Tathāgatas heard my lion’s roar, they all praised me and bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they also dispatched messengers so that the entire great assembly might see them.

I now make this final great vow to accomplish all the great compassion of a bodhisattva, until I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Once I have attained it, may all sentient beings who hear the name of my great compassion give rise to a sense of wonder. Furthermore, in future times, may those bodhisattvas who achieve great compassion likewise vow to take up such a world; for the sentient beings within that world who are famished for the Dharma, blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, and fully possessed by the four torrents—may these bodhisattvas act as their protectors and preach the Dharma for them.

Even after my parinirvāṇa, in every place throughout the immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds in the ten directions, may the Buddhas currently residing there, amidst their assemblies of bodhisattvas, praise my name and likewise proclaim my virtuous vows. May those bodhisattvas, through a mind of great compassion and diligence, all listen to these matters with single-minded focus, and upon hearing them, be greatly amazed and exclaim that such a thing has never been before.
The compassion previously attained shall all be further increased and expanded; according to my vow, I shall take hold of an impure land.

May all these bodhisattvas be like me, attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in impure worlds, pulling forth sentient beings from the four torrents, and establishing them securely within the three vehicles until they reach nirvāṇa.
“Good son! At that time, after the brahmin Ratnasāgara had contemplated such great compassionate vows, he bared his right shoulder and went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, there were again immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devas in the void, performing celestial music and raining down various kinds of flowers, each with a single voice praising him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent! Excellent, O Great Being!
You have now come before the Buddha to make a most extraordinary vow, desiring to extinguish the afflictions of the sentient beings in the world with the water of wisdom.
At that time, the entire great assembly joined their palms in reverence and, standing before the brahmin, prostrated with one voice and praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent! O Honored One of Great Wisdom!
We have now attained great benefit, being able to establish firm and steadfast vows for all that is wholesome.
"We now wish to hear the noble vows that have been inspired by your reverence.
At that time, the brahmin knelt with his right knee on the ground before the Buddha.

At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; various musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; birds and beasts sang in harmony with one another; and all the trees produced blossoms out of season. Within this trichiliocosm, among the sentient beings dwelling on the earth—whether they had already resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or had not yet done so—all except those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the lowly animals, gave rise to a mind of great benefit, a mind of pure goodness, a mind free from enmity or malice, a mind free from defilement or turbidity, and a mind of compassionate aspiration.

The flying beings immediately took their place in the air, their hearts filled with joy; they scattered various flowers, powdered incense, and unguents, and offered diverse musical instruments, banners, pennants, and robes as an act of worship. With soft and wondrous voices, they sang praises of the brahmin, all with single-minded intent desiring to hear the virtuous vows uttered by the brahmin.

Even the devas of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven descended to Jambudvīpa; remaining in the air, they scattered various flowers, powdered incense, and unguents, and offered various kinds of music, banners, pennants, and garments as an act of worship. With gentle and wondrous voices, they praised the brahmin, being single-mindedly diligent in their desire to hear the virtuous vows the brahmin had made.
At that time, the Brahmā-cakravartin Ratnasāgara joined his palms in reverence and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“Sporting in meditative concentration, you are like the Great Brahmā King;
Your radiant and majestic splendor is like Śakra, Lord of the Devas.”
Giving away wealth in charity is like a wheel-turning king;
Holding exquisite treasures is like a minister of the treasury;
Mastery over merit is like a lion king.
Unshakeable as Mount Sumeru; with a mind undisturbed like the waters of the great ocean;
regarding both transgression and non-transgression, his mind is like the earth.
Eliminating all afflictions, like pure water;
burning away all fetters and latent tendencies, like the fierce flames of fire;
free from all obstructions, like a great wind.
Manifesting the true Dharma like the Four Heavenly Kings;
raining down the rain of Dharma like the Great Dragon King;
satisfying all beings like the seasonal rains.
He vanquishes all non-Buddhists like a great master of treatises;
his wondrous voice of merit is like the sumana flower;
his wondrous voice of preaching the Dharma is like that of Brahmā.
Dispelling all suffering and affliction, like a great king of physicians;
regarding all with an impartial mind, like a mother’s love for her child;
gathering in sentient beings, like a compassionate father.
The body is indestructible, like a mountain of diamond;
it can sever the branches of craving, like a sharp blade;
it delivers beings widely from birth and death, like a ferryman.
Saving people through wisdom is like a boat;
his radiance is cool and refreshing, like the full moon;
he opens the flowers of sentient beings, like the rising sun.
He is able to bestow upon sentient beings the four fruits of the śramaṇa,
just as an autumn tree produces various fruits;
surrounded by sages and saints, he is like a phoenix.
His intention is profound and vast, like the great ocean;
he regards all sentient beings with an impartial mind, as if they were mere grass and trees;
he knows the characteristics of all phenomena as one observes an empty fist.
Walking through the world with an equanimous mind, level as the surface of water;
having perfected the wondrous marks and being skilled in great compassion,
he is able to bestow predictions of enlightenment upon immeasurable sentient beings.
I have now tamed immeasurable sentient beings;
I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me a prophecy that in a future age I shall accomplish the supreme path.
O World-Honored One, Great Sage of subtle and wondrous wisdom,
I pray that you will explain this with your sublime voice according to the truth.
In this degenerate age, I must cultivate all forms of patience.
Engaging in battle with the various fetters and afflictions,
he has uprooted immeasurable beings from them all,
establishing them securely within the path of tranquil extinction.
“Good son! When the brahmacārin Ratnasāgara had finished praising the Buddha with these verses, at that time the entire great assembly all exclaimed in praise: ‘Excellent!’”
Excellent! Great Man! You have skillfully praised the Tathāgata, the Dharma King.
At that time, the brahmin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I have already transformed and guided immeasurable billions of beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. These sentient beings have each vowed to take hold of pure and wondrous worlds, departing from impure lands; with pure minds they plant various roots of goodness, skillfully gathering in and subduing sentient beings."

The one thousand four hundred men, including Agniveśya Māṇava and others, all recited the non-Buddhist Vedas; the Tathāgata has already bestowed upon them the prediction that they shall become Buddhas within this Bhadrakalpa.
There are sentient beings who extensively practice greed, lust, anger, delusion, and arrogance; all such as these shall be tamed within the Three Vehicles.

As for those whom these one thousand four Buddhas have relinquished—namely, sentient beings with dense and heavy afflictions, who in this world of five turbidities commit the five heinous crimes, destroy the True Dharma, slander the sages, and engage in [evil deeds]...
Holding wrong views, they are deprived of the seven noble riches; they are unfilial toward their parents and lack respect in their hearts for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

They do what should not be done and fail to do what should be done; they do not perform meritorious deeds, they have no fear of future lives, and they have no desire to practice the three bases of merit, nor do they seek them.
Regarding the retributions among devas and humans, they diligently practice the ten unwholesome actions and head toward the three unwholesome realms.
Having distanced themselves from virtuous friends, they do not know how to draw near to true wisdom.

They enter the prison of birth and death within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*), drifting along with the four currents and sinking into the Ash River. Blinded by ignorance, they abandon all wholesome karma and focus [only on the unwholesome].

Having committed evil karma, such sentient beings are not tolerated within the worlds of the Buddhas; therefore, they have been banished and gathered here into this world. Because they have abandoned wholesome karma and practiced unwholesome deeds, the weight of their grave offenses on the false path has accumulated like a great mountain.

At that time, within the Bhadrakalpa of the Sahā world, the human lifespan was one thousand years. These fourteen Buddhas, out of great compassion, did not achieve [their enlightenment] in such a degenerate and evil age; they did not take birth in such a world where sentient beings wander through birth and death like mechanical puppets—without rescue or protection, without refuge, without shelter, and without light—suffering all manner of afflictions while being abandoned to their fate. Each of them instead vowed to take birth in a pure and wondrous world.

The sentient beings in the Pure Land have already disciplined themselves; their minds are pure, they have planted roots of goodness, and they practice with diligent vigor. Having already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, they are further gathered [into the Pure Land].
“World-Honored One! Is it truly so for these people?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin:
"It is truly as you have said, son of good family!
These individuals, according to their respective inclinations, each chose various adorned and pure worlds; I have accorded them predictions of enlightenment in accordance with their minds."
At that time, the brahmin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

My heart now trembles like the leaves of a *kiṃśuka* tree; my mind is filled with great sorrow and my body is utterly withered. Although these bodhisattvas have given rise to great compassion, they are unable to take up this world of the five turbidities; now those sentient beings have fallen into the darkness of ignorance.”
“World-Honored One!

Until the future, after one *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed and during the latter part of a second *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, when the human lifespan in the Bhadrakalpa is one thousand years, I shall at that time practice the bodhisattva path. Having long remained in birth and death and endured all sufferings, by the power of the samādhis of all bodhisattvas, I shall certainly not abandon such sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!
I now personally practice the six pāramitās to subdue sentient beings, in accordance with what the Buddha has said:
‘Giving material wealth is called dānapāramitā.’”
“World-Honored One!
When I practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), if there are sentient beings who from lifetime to lifetime beg from me for whatever they require,
I shall surely provide them with their requests in full— food and drink, medicine, clothing, and so forth.”
Bedding and seating, houses and villages, flowers and incense, necklaces and ornaments,
and scents for anointing the body; providing the sick with medicine, attendants, banners and streamers, precious parasols, money and grain,
silks and fabrics, elephants and horses, carriages, gold and silver, currency, pearls, lapis lazuli, and *vaiḍūrya*.
Pears, conch shells, jade disks, coral, genuine jewels, counterfeit gems, celestial crowns, and fly-whisks— regarding such objects as these,
I give them all away in great compassion even to those among sentient beings who are impoverished;
though I perform such giving, I do not seek the retribution of heavenly or human realms.
It is solely for the sake of taming and gathering sentient beings that, by such causes and conditions, he relinquishes all that he possesses.

If there are sentient beings who beg for excessive things—namely, slaves, villages, cities, wives, children, sons, daughters, hands, feet, noses, tongues, heads, eyes, skin, blood, bones, flesh, or even his own life—and who thus beg for such excessive objects.
At that time, I shall give rise to great compassion and offer these various things as alms, seeking no karmic reward, but solely for the sake of taming and gathering in sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!

When I practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), I surpass all past bodhisattvas who have practiced the perfection of giving, and I also surpass all future bodhisattvas who shall resolve to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and practice the perfection of giving.”
“World-Honored One!
For the sake of practicing the bodhisattva path in future ages, I shall practice such dānapāramitā for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas,
World-Honored One!”
"In future ages, if there should be those who wish to practice the Bodhisattva path, I shall for their sake practice the *dānapāramitā* so that it remains uninterrupted.

'When I first entered the *śīlapāramitā*, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I maintained various precepts and cultivated various ascetic practices as described in the section on *dāna*. Because I contemplated non-self (*anātman*), my five sense faculties were not harmed by the five sensory objects.'"

Regarding this perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), I practice this perfection of patience as described above: I contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) to remain free from all faults and evils, and I behold unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which are subtle, wondrous, and quiescent.
Diligently cultivating and accumulating [these virtues], one does not give rise to regression from the unsurpassed path.
This is the *vīryapāramitā*; I, too, practice this *vīryapāramitā* in such a manner.
If one practices the mark of emptiness in all places and attains the dharma of quiescence, this is called the dhyāna-pāramitā.
