There is the samādhi of non-obstruction; entering this samādhi, one encounters no obstruction among any phenomena.
There is the samādhi called "Free from Nets. Entering this samādhi, one sees that the foundations of all samādhis are free from high and low.
There is the samādhi called "Gathering All Meritorious Qualities. Entering this samādhi, one is free from the accumulation of all dharmas.
There is the samādhi of right abiding; entering this samādhi, one perceives neither mind nor mental factors among all phenomena.
There is the samādhi of awakening; entering this samādhi, one is immediately able to awaken to all phenomena.
There is the samādhi of mindful discernment; entering this samādhi, one attains immeasurable eloquence regarding all phenomena.
There is the samādhi of pure wisdom-awakening; entering this samādhi, one attains equality and non-equality regarding all phenomena.
There is the samādhi of the characteristic of wisdom; entering this samādhi, one is able to transcend the triple world.
There is the samādhi of the severance of wisdom; entering this samādhi, one perceives the severance of all dharmas.
There is the Wisdom-Rain Samādhi; entering this samādhi, one obtains the rain of all dharmas.
There is the Non-Reliance Samādhi; entering this samādhi, one perceives no basis for reliance among all dharmas.
There is the Samādhi of Great Adornment; entering this samādhi, one does not perceive the banner of dharmas among all dharmas.
There is the Samādhi of Practice; entering this samādhi, one is able to see that all dharmas are entirely quiescent in their practice.
There is the samādhi called "Transcending All Conditioned Phenomena," by entering which one thoroughly penetrates and understands all dharmas.
There is the samādhi called "Vernacular Speech," by entering which one is able to understand vernacular speech.
There is the samādhi of being free from language and devoid of words; entering this samādhi, one fully understands that among all phenomena there are no linguistic expressions.
There is the samādhi of the torch of wisdom; entering this samādhi, one is able to provide illumination regarding all phenomena.
There is the samādhi of the Lion’s Roar of Superior Wisdom; entering this samādhi, one manifests the mark of purity within all phenomena.
There is the samādhi of the Mark of Penetrating Wisdom; entering this samādhi, one perceives the mark of wisdom in all phenomena.
There is the samādhi called Accomplishing All Practices; entering this samādhi, one accomplishes all practices among all dharmas.
There is the samādhi called Detachment from Suffering and Pleasure; entering this samādhi, one has no point of reliance among all dharmas.
There is the Samādhi of Inexhaustible Practice; entering this samādhi, one sees that all dharmas are inexhaustible.
There is the Dhāraṇī Samādhi; entering this samādhi, one is able to maintain the characteristics of dharmas within all samādhis, perceiving neither the deviant nor the correct.
There is the samādhi of neither aversion nor attachment; entering this samādhi, one perceives neither aversion nor attachment among all phenomena.
There is the samādhi of pure light; entering this samādhi, one does not perceive any defilement within conditioned phenomena.
There is the Samādhi of Firmness; entering this samādhi, one does not perceive any phenomena that lack firmness.
There is the Samādhi of the Pure Light of the Full Moon; entering this samādhi, one is able to fully accomplish and perfect all merits.
There is the Samādhi of Great Adornment; entering this samādhi, one perceives within all samādhis the accomplishment of immeasurable adornments.
There is the Samādhi of Universal World-Illumination; entering this samādhi, one illuminates all samādhis with wisdom.
There is the samādhi of universal equal illumination; entering this samādhi, one attains single-mindedness within all samādhis.
There is the samādhi of purity and non-purity; entering this samādhi, one perceives neither purity nor impurity within all samādhis.
There is the samādhi called "Houseless"; entering this samādhi, one does not perceive the houses of any samādhis.
There is the samādhi called "Suchness"; entering this samādhi, one perceives neither action nor non-action among all phenomena.
There is the Samādhi of the Non-existence of Body; entering this samādhi, one does not perceive the existence of a body among all phenomena.
Bodhisattvas attain such gates of samādhi as these: their vocal karma is pure like space, and within all phenomena they do not perceive vocal karma, being without obstruction just like space.
O Mahākāruṇika!
These are called the gateways to the samādhis of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in the Mahāyāna.
*Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
The Sutra of the Compassionate Lotus, Scroll Nine, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Five: The Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā), Part Two.
“‘Good son! What is the gate of purification for the factors that assist the bodhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Good son!...’”
Generosity is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it transforms sentient beings.
Ethical discipline is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it fulfills virtuous vows.
Patience is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it fulfills the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Diligence is a factor that aids the realization of enlightenment, for it involves the tireless teaching and transformation of all sentient beings.
Meditative concentration is a factor that aids the realization of enlightenment, for it causes the mind to become fully disciplined and subdued.
Wisdom is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it possesses the capacity to fully understand all afflictions.
Extensive learning is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it possesses unimpeded mastery regarding all phenomena.
All merits are factors that assist the awakening, because all sentient beings attain their fulfillment through them.
The activity of wisdom is a factor that assists the awakening, because one attains the fulfillment of unimpeded wisdom.
The cultivation of meditative concentration is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it brings about the complete accomplishment of a supple mind.
The activity of wisdom is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it brings one far away from all doubts and perplexities.
The mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is a factor that assists in awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), for the mind toward all sentient beings is free from obstruction.
The mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) is a factor that assists in awakening, for it extracts sentient beings from all their sufferings.
The mind of joy is a factor that assists toward enlightenment, because it experiences the Dharma of bliss.
The mind of equanimity is a factor that assists toward enlightenment, because it severs both hatred and attachment.
Listening to the Dharma is a factor that assists toward enlightenment, because it severs the five hindrances.
Transcending the world is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it involves relinquishing all that one possesses.
Dwelling in an araṇya is a factor conducive to enlightenment, for it is free from all worldly busyness.
Single-minded mindfulness is a factor that aids the awakening of bodhi, for it results in the attainment of dhāraṇī.
Right mindfulness is a factor that aids the awakening of bodhi, for it involves the discernment of mental consciousness.
Contemplation (*cintā*) is an auxiliary to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), because it achieves the realization of the meaning within all phenomena.
The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are auxiliary to the factors of enlightenment, because they involve the discernment of the awakening to body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Right effort is a factor conducive to enlightenment, because it abandons unwholesome dharmas and cultivates wholesome dharmas.
The bases of psychic power are factors conducive to enlightenment, because they render the body and mind supple and agile.
The faculties (*indriya*) are themselves factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), because they bring about the perfection of the faculties of all sentient beings.
The powers (*bala*) are themselves factors conducive to enlightenment, because they possess the capacity to utterly destroy all afflictions (*kleśa*).
All forms of awakening are factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), because they fully realize the true characteristics of phenomena among all dharmas.
The right path is a factor conducive to enlightenment, because it remains far removed from all erroneous paths.
The Noble Truths are factors conducive to enlightenment, for they bring about the total cessation of all afflictions.
The four analytical knowledges are factors conducive to enlightenment, for they enable one to sever the doubts of sentient beings.
Mindfulness through conditions is a factor that aids awakening, for it is by not hearing from others that one attains wisdom.
A virtuous friend is a factor that aids awakening, for all merits are uniquely accomplished thereby.
The arousal of the thought of enlightenment is a factor that aids awakening, for it accomplishes the non-deception of all sentient beings.
The application of mental attention is a factor that aids awakening, for it brings forth all phenomena.
Single-minded concentration is a factor that aids enlightenment, for it increases wholesome dharmas.
Contemplation of wholesome dharmas is a factor that aids enlightenment, for it brings to fulfillment whatever dharmas one has heard.
Gathering [these teachings] is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it brings about the transformation and education of all sentient beings.
Upholding the true Dharma is a factor that aids the path to enlightenment, for it ensures that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed.
Virtuous vows are factors that assist the realization of enlightenment, for they bring about the accomplishment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field.
Skillful means are factors that assist the realization of enlightenment, for they lead to the swift attainment of all-knowledge.
"Good son! This is called the *Sūtra on the Pure Gate of the Dharmas that Assist Bodhi for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas*. Good son!"
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha looked all around at the great assembly of bodhisattvas and addressed Mahākāruṇika, saying:
"Mahākāruṇika! How does a bodhisattva, adorned with the ornaments of fearlessness, become fully endowed with patience?"
“Good son! If a bodhisattva perceives the ultimate truth (paramārtha), he attains non-deluded diligence and does not cling to the triple world.

If he does not cling to the triple world, this is called the fearless śramaṇa-dharma of samādhi; it is like moving one’s hand in empty space, where there is nothing to which one clings, and furthermore, it is like observing all dharmas without perceiving their characteristics.”
O Great Compassionate One!
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s adornment of the necklace of fearlessness.
O son of good family!
How does a bodhisattva fulfill patience?

When such a bodhisattva dwells in the Dharma, they do not perceive any phenomena as having even the appearance of a minute particle. They contemplate all phenomena in both their direct and reverse orders and understand that within them there is no karmic retribution. In practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they realize there is no self; in practicing compassion (*karuṇā*), they realize there are no sentient beings; in practicing sympathetic joy (*muditā*), they realize there is no life-principle; and in practicing equanimity (*upekṣā*), they realize there is no person.
Although one practices giving, one does not perceive the gift.
Although one practices ethical discipline, one does not perceive a pure mind.
Although one practices patience, one does not perceive sentient beings.
Although one practices diligence, there is no mind of detachment from desire.
Although one practices meditative concentration, there is no mind of eliminating evil.
Although one practices wisdom, the mind has nothing upon which to act.
Although one practices the foundations of mindfulness, one does not perceive discursive thought.
Although one practices the right efforts, one does not perceive the arising and ceasing of the mind.
Although one practices the bases of psychic power, one does not perceive the immeasurable mind.
Although they practice faith, they do not perceive a mind free from obstacles.
Although they practice mindfulness, they do not perceive a mind that has attained mastery.
Although they practice concentration, they do not perceive a mind entering meditative absorption.
Although they practice wisdom, they do not perceive a faculty of wisdom.
Although they practice the powers, there is nothing to be destroyed.
Although they practice the factors of enlightenment, their minds are free from discrimination.
Although one practices the path of righteousness, one does not perceive all phenomena.
Although one practices the karma of meditative concentration, one does not perceive the stillness of the mind.
Although one practices the karma of wisdom, one does not perceive that which the mind engages.
Although they practice the Noble Truths, they do not perceive a dharma-characteristic through which they attain penetration.
Although they cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha, they do not perceive a mind of immeasurable practices.
Although they cultivate mindfulness of the Dharma, their minds are equal to the Dharma-realm.
Although they cultivate mindfulness of the Sangha, their minds abide nowhere; they purify their minds through the teaching and transformation of sentient beings.
Although they uphold the True Dharma, their minds do not engage in discrimination regarding the various dharma-realms.
Although he cultivates the Pure Land, his mind is as impartial as empty space.
Although he cultivates the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha, his mind is free from all signs.
Although he attains patience, his mind has nothing whatsoever.
Although they abide in non-retrogression, they never perceive for themselves either retrogression or non-retrogression.
Although they practice at the site of enlightenment, they understand that the three realms possess no distinct characteristics.
Although they destroy all demons, this is truly for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings.
Although they practice for enlightenment, they contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena and possess no bodhicitta.
Although they turn the wheel of Dharma, regarding all phenomena there is neither turning nor returning.
Although they further manifest great parinirvāṇa, within the midst of birth and death their minds remain equal and without distinction.
"This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience.

When this Dharma was being spoken, sixty-four billion Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas came from the ten directions to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, to hear this *Sūtra on the Pure Gate of the Dharma that Assists Enlightenment through the Samādhi of Original Causes*. Having heard this Dharma, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly:

"You should now know that when the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha preached this Dharma in ages past, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the sands of forty-eight Ganges Rivers who attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti); bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms of the four continents dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression; and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the sands of one Ganges River attained this Sūtra on the Pure Gate of the Dharma for Aiding Bodhi, namely the Samādhi of Fundamental Conditions."

"Good son! At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā felt joy in his heart and immediately underwent a transformation of his body; his appearance was like that of a twenty-year-old man, and he followed the Tathāgata as a shadow follows a form."

"Good son! At that time, the wheel-turning sage king, his thousand sons, eighty-four thousand minor kings, and nine hundred and twenty million people all left the household life together. They upheld the prohibitive precepts, cultivated extensive learning, practiced patience and samādhi, and applied themselves with diligent vigor."

“Good son! At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahākaruṇā gradually received from the Buddha the eighty-four thousand dharma-aggregates pertaining to the śrāvakas and the ninety thousand dharma-aggregates pertaining to the pratyekabuddhas; he took them up, maintained them, recited them, and mastered them all thoroughly.”

Within the Mahāyāna treasury of the Dharma, he fully received, upheld, recited, and mastered one hundred thousand clusters of teachings in the mindfulness of the body, one hundred thousand clusters of teachings in the mindfulness of sensation, one hundred thousand clusters of teachings in the mindfulness of mind, and one hundred thousand clusters of teachings in the mindfulness of phenomena.

Within the eighteen *dhātus*, there are one hundred thousand clusters of dharmas; within the twelve *āyatanas*, there are one hundred thousand clusters of dharmas; there are one hundred thousand clusters of dharmas for severing desire, one hundred thousand clusters of dharmas for severing hatred, and one hundred thousand clusters of dharmas for severing delusion; there are one hundred thousand clusters of dharmas for samādhi and liberation, and one hundred thousand clusters of dharmas for the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). All such ten billion clusters of dharmas he fully receives, maintains, recites, and masters.

“Good son! Subsequently, when that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, at that time the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahākāruṇika made offerings with immeasurable and boundless varieties of flowers, powdered incense, ointment incense, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, rare treasures, and musical instruments. He used various piles of incense as fuel to cremate the body, collected the relics, and erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances, five yojanas in height and one yojana in both length and breadth, being perfectly symmetrical.”
For seven days, they further made offerings with various kinds of immeasurable and boundless flowers, incense, music, precious banners, flags, and canopies.
At that time, he further caused immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to dwell securely within the teachings of the Three Vehicles. "Good son!

After seven days have passed, the Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā, together with eighty-four thousand people, will leave the household life, shave off his hair and beard, and don the dyed *kāṣāya*. Following the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he will, in accordance with an impartial mind, cause the True Dharma to blaze brightly for ten thousand years. He will further cause immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings to dwell securely within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, as well as in the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, the Eightfold Fast, and the Ten Precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*, until they gradually fulfill the pure conduct of the great *bhikṣu*."

Furthermore, he exhorted and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, establishing them securely in the four immeasurable practices through the skillful means of supernormal powers. He led them to contemplate the five aggregates as being like hostile thieves, to contemplate the sense bases as being like an empty village, and to contemplate conditioned phenomena as arising from causes and conditions. He exhorted and transformed these sentient beings so that they might attain knowledge and vision, contemplating all phenomena as being like reflections in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, and like the moon in water; thus, within all phenomena, they came to know that there is no self, no birth, and no cessation—the supreme, tranquil, and subtle nirvana.
Furthermore, having caused immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to dwell securely within the Eightfold Noble Path and having thus performed such great benefits, he then passed away.

Immediately thereafter, there were again immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of people who made various offerings to the relics of the Bhikṣu of Great Compassion. All their offerings were exactly according to the rites of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin King); the manner in which this great multitude offered various gifts to the relics of the Bhikṣu of Great Compassion was likewise so.

On the day the Great Compassionate Bhikṣu passed away, all the True Dharma of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha was extinguished without remainder on that very same day. Due to their original vows, those bodhisattvas were born in various Buddha-fields, or among the Tuṣita devas, or among humans, or among nāgas; or among yakṣas, or among asuras, or they were born among various kinds of animals.

“Good son! After the Bhikṣu Mahākaruṇā passed away, by virtue of his original vow, ten thousand Buddha-lands to the south of here there was a Buddha-world named Joyful Delight (*Ratiprīti*). The people therein had a lifespan of eighty years; they accumulated all roots of unwholesomeness, delighted in killing, dwelt securely in various evils, lacked compassion for sentient beings, were unfilial toward their parents, and even did not fear future worlds.”

Due to his original vow, the Bhikṣu of Great Compassion was born into a family of caṇḍālas in that world. His physical body was tall and well-proportioned, and his strength was fierce, formidable, and courageous. He was single-mindedly attentive, possessed swift eloquence in debate, and in all such matters surpassed ordinary men. Using his great power and force, he would seize people and say to them:

"If you can now accept the precept against stealing, and even distance yourselves from various wrong views to practice right view, I shall grant you your life, provide you with all necessary assets and wealth, and ensure you lack for nothing."
"If you do not accept [this], I shall now certainly sever the life-faculty of you, and only then depart.
At that time, those people knelt for a long time with palms joined and spoke these words:
"O Benevolent One!"
Now that you have disciplined me, I shall uphold what you have instructed; for the rest of my life, I will no longer commit theft, and this shall likewise apply to everything up to right view.
"At that time, the powerful Caṇḍāla went to the king or to a great minister and spoke these words:

'I am now destitute of the means of livelihood, namely food and drink, medicine, clothing, bedding, incense and flowers, gold and silver, money and goods, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, amber, true gems, and counterfeit gems.'"
"If I obtain these various kinds of things, I shall take them and give them as gifts to sentient beings.
At that time, the king and his ministers immediately provided him with all the various necessities required to make him fully satisfied.
At that time, because of that gift, the caṇḍāla established the king and his ministers in the nine wholesome states.
Then, the lifespan of the people increased until it reached five hundred years. When that king passed away, the ministers succeeded him to the throne and gave him the name Puṇyabala (Power of Merit).

“Good son! At that time, King Guṇabala will first rule over one kingdom; then, by virtue of his power, he will rule over two kingdoms. In this manner, before long, he will even attain the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) ruling over Jambudvīpa. Thereafter, he will teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing them in the precept of non-killing; it shall be the same for everything up to right view. According to the inclinations and aspirations of sentient beings, he will exhort and transform them, causing them to abide within the Three Vehicles.”
At that time, after King Guṇabala had taught immeasurable sentient beings within Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action and the three vehicles, he proclaimed aloud throughout Jambudvīpa:
"If there are those who beg or require food and drink, or even wish to obtain various kinds of rare treasures, let them all come here; I shall provide and bestow them upon you."
At that time, all the mendicants within Jambudvīpa, having heard this proclamation, assembled together.
Then King Guṇabala provided them with various necessities according to their wishes, satisfying them all.
At that time, there was a Nirgrantha named Pāṃśuśravas who went to the king’s presence and spoke these words:

“The various great gifts you are now bestowing to seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path—I now require that which you should grant me so that my needs may be fulfilled; in a future age, you shall cause the lamp of the Dharma to blaze brightly.”
Then the king asked, "What do you require? The man replied:
"I have been reciting and maintaining mantras, desiring to engage in battle with those asuras; fearing their destruction and seeking victory for myself, I have reported these matters to the King."
"What is required is the skin and eyes of one who is not yet dead.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King reflected thus:

"Now that I have obtained this immeasurable power as a Wheel-Turning Sage King, I have established immeasurable sentient beings in the ten wholesome paths and the Three Vehicles, and I have further performed immeasurable and boundless great acts of giving. This spiritual friend wishes to cause me to trade this non-durable body for a durable body."
At that time, the Great King spoke these words:
"You should now give rise to a heart of joy; I shall now bestow upon you this ordinary human flesh eye."
By this cause and condition, may I attain the pure eye of wisdom in future lives.
Having peeled off my skin and given it to you with a joyful heart, by this further cause and condition, may I, after attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, obtain a body of golden hue.
"Good son! At that time, King Guṇabala plucked out both his eyes with his right hand and gave them to the Nirgrantha. As blood flowed and stained his face, he spoke these words:
'All you devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—whether you dwell in the void or upon the earth—listen all to my words.'"

All that I now give as alms is for the sake of the path to unsurpassed bodhi and pure nirvāṇa, to deliver all sentient beings from the four currents of saṃsāra, and to enable them to find rest and abide in nirvāṇa.
He further spoke these words:

"If it is certain that I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then even though I perform this act, my life-force should not be severed or destroyed, I should not lose right mindfulness, and I should feel no regret, such that the incantations performed by the Nirgrantha may succeed."
He further said: "Come now, you may strip off my skin.
O son of good family!
At that time, the Nirgrantha took a sharp blade and flayed the king’s skin; after seven days had passed, the spells he had cast were all fully accomplished.
During those seven days, the great king’s life did not end, and he did not lose his right mindfulness; although he endured such suffering, not even a single thought of regret arose within him.
“Good son! You should know now:
as for that Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā at that time, could he possibly have been anyone else?
Do not view it thus; he was none other than myself.”

In a past life, in the presence of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he first resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having first resolved his mind, he exhorted and transformed immeasurable and boundless sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Good son! This was my first courageous and vigorous exertion. At that time, by the power of my original vow, at the end of my life I was born into a family of caṇḍālas in the world of Joyful Delight; this was my second courageous and vigorous exertion.”

I was born into a family of caṇḍālas, yet I taught sentient beings in the midst of wholesome dharmas; by the power of my own strength, I even attained the status of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), extinguishing the strife and defilement of Jambudvīpa, bringing about tranquility and increasing the lifespan of beings—this was the first time I gave away my skin and my eyes.

"Good son! By the power of my vow, after passing away from that life, I returned once more to be born in the world of Joyful Delight (*Sukhāvatī*) into the family of a *caṇḍāla*. Eventually, I attained the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and by means of my great power, I established sentient beings within the wholesome Dharma. In that world, I further eliminated the matters of bandits, strife, and defilement, causing all sentient beings to increase in their lifespan. It was at that time that I finally relinquished my tongue and ears."
Having thus performed such great benefits in each and every world-system within that trichiliocosm, by the power of his vows, his diligence remains firm in this successive manner.

Furthermore, in as many worlds of the five turbidities and evil ages as there are sands in this single Ganges River, he brings great benefit, establishing sentient beings in wholesome dharmas and the Three Vehicles, and eliminating enemies, strife, and defilement.
"Good son!

Furthermore, in all other pure worlds of the ten directions, when the various Buddhas were originally practicing the path toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they did not speak of the faults of others, nor did they utter harsh or evil words to others; they did not manifest terrors through the use of forceful power, nor did they encourage sentient beings toward the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, having fully accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these Buddhas have attained these pure, wondrous, and excellent worlds, which are free from the names of offenses and where there is no need for receiving precepts. Their ears never hear harsh or evil words; there are no unwholesome sounds, but only the sound of the Dharma is constantly heard, being free from all unpleasant sounds. They have attained mastery over all sentient beings, and even the names of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not exist there.

“Good son! During kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges that were devoid of Buddhas and possessed of the five turbidities, I terrified sentient beings by using harsh and evil words and causing them to lose their lives. Only thereafter did I exhort them to dwell securely in wholesome dharmas and within the Three Vehicles. Because of this residual karma, I have come to obtain such a corrupt and evil world, where unwholesome sounds resound throughout the entire realm; therefore, I now find a world filled with unwholesome sentient beings. By preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, I fulfill my original vow to take hold of a Buddha-world to tame sentient beings, and such is the manner of its accomplishment.”

I have diligently practiced and cultivated the path to enlightenment as described; therefore, I have now attained a Buddha-field resembling a seed, just as I originally vowed. Thus, my original vow has now been fulfilled.
“Good son! Now I shall briefly describe the *dānapāramitā* I practiced in the past.

When I practiced the *dānapāramitā*, there were none among the bodhisattvas of the past who, while practicing the bodhisattva path, could practice such a practice as this; nor will there be any among those who practice the bodhisattva path in future ages who can practice such a practice.”
When I was practicing the perfection of giving as a bodhisattva, I excluded only eight virtuous men of the past:

the first bodhisattva was named Ekabhūmiprāpta. He attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment here in the southern land of Sarvadoṣa, where he was known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, the Radiance that Shatters Afflictions. The lifespan of humans there was one hundred years, and while he taught the Dharma therein, seven days later he entered parinirvāṇa.

The second bodhisattva was named Pure Diligence (*Vīryaviśuddha*). In this eastern land of Blazing Flames (*Jvalanajvālā*), he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and was named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān known as Guṇa. The human lifespan there was one hundred years; within that time he taught the Dharma and performed the work of a Buddha. After that Buddha had passed through a period of great eons (*mahākalpa*) equal in number to the sands of one Ganges River, he entered unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. The relics of that Buddha remain until this very day, performing the work of a Buddha in a land where no other Buddha resides, no differently than I do.

The third bodhisattva was named Dṛḍhaketu; he applied himself with diligent vigor to all samādhis and practiced giving with great power. In a future age, after ten *gaṅgā*-sands of great kalpas have passed, he will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* here in the northern world-realm called Sukhāvatī, where he shall be known as King Vichinnatṛṣṇā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

The fourth bodhisattva was named Prajñājvala-saṃgraha-pramoda. After one great kalpa had passed, he attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) in this western world-system called Bhīṣma, where the lifespan of humans was one hundred years. There, he became known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān, named Sūryagarbha-prabhā-vimala-guṇarāja.
Before me now stand two bodhisattvas: the first named Sūryaprabha and the second named Priyabāhu.

In a future age, after the passage of immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, in this world-system above called Asha-smoke (Pāṃśu-dhūma), during a kalpa named Great Turmoil, in an evil world of the five turbidities filled with many afflictions, when the human lifespan is five...
After ten years, by virtue of his original vow, the Bodhisattva Sunlight attained unexcelled,
perfect, and complete enlightenment therein, receiving the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, named Inconceivable Sunlight.
The Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will fulfill his buddha-activities for a full ten years and then enter parinirvāṇa;
on the very day of his nirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall also perish. Thereafter, for ten years, there will be no Buddha and time will pass in vain.
The lifespan of humans will further diminish until it reaches thirty years, at which point the Bodhisattva Priyabhuja, by virtue of his original vow, [will appear].
Therefore, therein he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and was named the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-sampanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Jayasūryaprabha. He—
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, likewise fulfilled his buddha-activities over the course of ten years and then entered parinirvāṇa;
having entered parinirvāṇa, by virtue of his original vow, the True Dharma remained in the world for a full seventy years.

At that time, the two bodhisattvas were before me; having just received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they felt great joy in their hearts upon hearing the prediction and prostrated themselves in reverent salutation.
Out of joy, they ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees; with palms joined toward the Buddha, they spoke in unison, reciting these verses:
“The radiance of the Tathāgata surpasses that of the sun and moon;
In this evil world, he can manifest great wisdom.”
The Tamer with pure eyes, free from all defilement,
Subdues the non-Buddhists through sublime discourse.
For immeasurable kalpas, I have cultivated the concentration of signlessness.
In seeking the unsurpassed, supreme, and wondrous Bodhi,
I made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
yet the Buddhas of the past did not bestow upon me a prediction of enlightenment.
The World-Honored One has transcended desire and attained liberation of mind;
in this dark age, he skillfully performs the work of a Buddha.
For the sake of all sentient beings who have lost their way, he preaches the Dharma.
May all be enabled to escape from drifting in birth and death.
This is my present aspiration: to attain mastery herein, and within this pure Buddha-dharma, to leave the household life and cultivate the Way.
With pure precepts leading to liberation, practicing exactly as taught,
their concentrated minds follow the Buddha like a shadow follows a form.
Not for the sake of gain or sustenance, they seek only the True Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, I have partaken of the flavor of ambrosia.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has granted me this prediction:
that in a future age, I shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
“Good son! The other two persons have not yet resolved their minds [on enlightenment].
Those who have already resolved their minds are: first, named Sūryaprabha (Sunlight), and second, named Priyabāhu (Joyful Arm).”

Formerly there were four people: the first was named Prthivīprāpta, the second Vīryaviśuddha, the third Dṛḍhaketu, and the fourth Prajñājvalanasaṃgraha-pramudita. Together there were eight people; these six bodhisattvas were those whom I first exhorted to resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! Listen now attentively to the causes and conditions of the past.

Innumerable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, at that time, this world was named Vimala-Sumeru, and the human lifespan was one hundred years. A Buddha appeared in the world, named Gandhapadma; after his parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, I was at that time a Great Powerful Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), named Durjayadhvaja.”

The King of Jambudvīpa possessed a full thousand sons, all of whom I exhorted and transformed, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subsequently, within the Buddha-dharma of the image of the Incense Lotus Flower Buddha, they left the household life to practice the Way, fervently increasing and propagating the Tathāgata’s bequeathed teachings; with the sole exception of six sons, who were unwilling to leave the household life or resolve upon *bodhicitta*.
At that time, I repeatedly addressed them, saying: "Sirs!
What do you now seek to obtain?"
"Why do you not resolve to attain the unsurpassed path, leave the household life, and practice the Way?
At that time, the six sons spoke these words:
"We should not leave the household life."

Why is this? If one leaves the household life during the final age of the Semblance Dharma and is unable to achieve the fulfillment of the aggregate of precepts, one will be deprived of the seven noble riches. Because of failing to guard the precepts, such a person sinks into the mire of birth and death, falls into the three evil realms, and cannot attain rebirth among gods or humans.
"For these reasons, we are unable to leave the household life to practice the Way. "Good son!
I asked again:"
"Why do you not resolve to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment?
The six sons replied,
"If you can grant us Jambudvīpa, then we shall resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Good son! Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy, and I thought to myself:

'I have now transformed the people of Jambudvīpa, establishing them in the Three Refuges, causing them to receive the Eight Precepts, and settling them in the Three Vehicles. I shall now divide this Jambudvīpa into six parts and give them to these six sons, so that they may give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment; thereafter, I shall leave the household life to cultivate the Way. "
Having reflected thus, he divided Jambudvīpa into six portions according to his intention and bestowed them upon his sons; he then immediately went forth into the homeless life.
At that time, the six kings were each at variance with one another; they did not accord with or obey one another, but instead plundered, attacked, fought, quarreled, bound, and shackled each other.

At that time, within all of Jambudvīpa, the crops failed to ripen and the people suffered from famine; rain did not fall at its proper seasons, and all the trees withered away, producing neither flowers nor fruit. Medicinal herbs did not grow, and the people, beasts, and winged birds were all famished, their bodies burning as if they were masses of fire.
At that time, I further reflected to myself:
"I should now sacrifice my own body—its flesh, skin, blood, and marrow—to give to sentient beings so that they may be fully satisfied."

Having formed this thought, he departed from his hermitage in the araṇya and went among the people. On the way, there was a mountain named Jalapriya; staying upon that mountain, he made this vow and spoke these verses:
"Just as I have renounced my own life and body out of great compassion, seeking no karmic reward, [so shall I act for the sake of all beings]."
"Only for the benefit of all devas and humans,
I vow to become a mountain of flesh to provide for and give to sentient beings.
That which I now relinquish is my exquisite form, so beautiful and dignified."
Seeking neither Śakra, nor the Māra kings, nor the Brahmā kings,
but solely for the benefit of future humans and devas,
I offer this flesh and blood as a gift to all sentient beings.
All you devas, nāgas, and spirits, humans and non-humans alike who dwell in the mountains and forests, listen now to my words:
for the sake of all sentient beings, I have given rise to great compassion.
"I shall give of my own flesh and blood to provide for them.
"O son of good family!

When I had made this vow at that time, the various devas were moved with agitation, and the great earth, all the mountains, Mount Sumeru, and the great oceans all shook in six ways; the great assemblies of humans and devas raised their voices in piteous wailing."
At that time, on Mount Jalaprabha, I threw myself down from it; by the power of my vow, I immediately became a mountain of flesh, one yojana in height, and exactly one yojana in length and breadth.
At that time, humans, birds, and beasts began for the first time to eat flesh and drink blood.

By virtue of their original vows, during the middle watch of the night, they increased and expanded their bodies until they reached a height of one thousand yojanas, with a length and breadth of exactly one thousand yojanas as well; on their sides, human heads naturally grew, complete with hair, eyebrows, eyes, ears, noses, mouths, lips, and tongues.
Within each of those heads, a voice arose proclaiming these words:

"May all sentient beings, each according to their own desire, take and use as they please—drinking blood, eating flesh, and taking heads, eyes, ears, noses, lips, tongues, teeth, and so forth—until they are fully satisfied; thereafter, may they all resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or resolve upon the mind of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*."
"O you! You should know that such things as these are all inexhaustible; they are easily digested when eaten and do not shorten one's lifespan.

"There are those of clear wisdom who eat meat and drink blood, and from those who take their heads, eyes, ears, noses, or tongues, some may resolve toward the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, some may resolve toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and some may seek the wealth and pleasures of gods and humans."

By virtue of his original vow, his body shall suffer no diminution until he reaches ten thousand years of age; meanwhile, all people within Jambudvīpa, as well as spirits, deities, birds, and beasts, shall be fully satisfied.

Throughout ten thousand years, the eyes he gave away were as numerous as the sands of a single Ganges River; the blood he gave was like the waters of the four great oceans; the flesh he relinquished was like a thousand Mount Sumerus; the tongues he relinquished were like the Great Iron Ring Mountains; the ears he relinquished were like Mount Cūḍālā; the noses he relinquished were like Mount Vipula; the teeth he relinquished were like Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; and the skin of his body he relinquished was equal to all the earth within the trichiliocosm.

“Good son! You should now know that during the ten thousand years of my past, I have relinquished immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodies. Within each single lifetime, I personally gave my own flesh and blood as alms to such immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings, causing them all to be fully satisfied, without ever giving rise to a single thought of regret.”
At that time, I spoke these words again:
"If it is certain that I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and if my vow is fulfilled so that I may obtain my own benefit,
then within these ten thousand years of this single Jambudvīpa, by myself..."

He gave his flesh and blood to all immeasurable sentient beings; for ten thousand years, equal in number to the sands of one Ganges River, he filled this stainless Sumeru trichiliocosm with mountains of flesh and blood.
Throughout each world-system during those ten thousand years, he personally gave his own flesh, blood, head, eyes, ears, and so forth.
They bestow gifts upon sentient beings— namely devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, humans, and non-humans, as well as all animals,
whether dwelling in the air or on the ground, even down to the hungry ghosts— causing them all to be fully satisfied;
thereafter, they exhort and transform them, establishing them within the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

If, having fully satisfied the sentient beings throughout this single Buddha-world, one then proceeds to as many worlds of the five turbidities in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and further provides blood, flesh, head, eyes, ears, and so forth, bestowing them upon sentient beings until all are fully satisfied.
In this manner, throughout as many great kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, for the sake of sentient beings, I shall sacrifice my own body and life to give them away.

If my vow is not fulfilled and I do not attain my own benefit, I would then be deceiving the immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions who turn the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings; I would certainly fail to achieve Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and remain within birth and death, never hearing the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, the sound of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha, the sound of the pāramitās, the sound of the powers and fearlessnesses, nor even the sound of any roots of goodness whatsoever.
"If I cannot achieve the perfection of giving my body as an offering to satisfy all sentient beings, may I always fall into the Avīci Hell. "Good son!

In the past, all such vows as these were fully accomplished by me; in every single world-system, I gave up my own body’s flesh and blood, bestowing them upon sentient beings so that they were all fully satisfied.

In this manner, proceeding in succession, he filled Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, relinquishing his own body’s flesh and blood to give to sentient beings, causing them all to be fully satisfied.

“Good son! You should now know that at that time, for the sake of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), I sacrificed my body in acts of charity; in this manner, I successively gave away my eyes until their mass filled this Jambudvīpa, reaching as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”
"Good son! This is called the Tathāgata’s brief explanation of the perfection of giving through the relinquishment of the body. Furthermore, good son!"
Thus, after the passing of further immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this world was renamed Candravajra and was likewise a world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

At that time, I became a *cakravartin* king ruling over Jambudvīpa, named Pradīpaprabha. I also instructed immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable people, establishing them in all wholesome dharmas, just as described above.
Having done this, I wandered through the gardens and groves, surveying the land, when I saw a man bound in fetters. I immediately asked him:
"What offense has he committed?"
The minister replied, "Of all the grain and wheat obtained from agricultural labor, it should be divided into six parts, with one part going to the government.
This man has not obeyed the royal law and was unwilling to deliver his share; for this reason, he has been bound."
At that time, I immediately issued an order to release him, saying: "From this day forward, you must not forcibly seize anyone.
The minister replied:
"Among these people, there is not even a single person who gives rise to a heart of joy and escorts him away out of a sense of righteousness."

Now, as for these princes, the members of the inner palace, the nobles, and the court ladies, as well as all their provisions and utensils for food and drink—all have been forcibly seized from others; there is not a single person who has given them with a pure mind.
"Having heard this, my heart was filled with great sorrow, and I thought to myself:
'To whom in this Jambudvīpa should I entrust this?
At that time, I had five hundred sons, whom I had previously inspired to resolve upon the unsurpassed path."

"I shall divide this land into five hundred equal portions and bestow them upon my sons; I, however, shall go forth into homelessness to dwell in an araṇya, practice the dharmas of the sages, and train in the pure conduct of Brahma."

Having reflected thus, he immediately divided this land into five hundred portions and gave them equally to his sons; he then went forth into homelessness and, reaching the great forest of *Udumbara* trees on the shore of the southern ocean, subsisted on various fruits while gradually practicing and training until he attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
“Good son! At that time, there were five hundred merchants in Jambudvīpa who entered the great ocean desiring to gather precious jewels.

There was a merchant leader named Pūrṇacandra; by virtue of the merit and conditions from his previous lives, he reached the jewel-island according to his wishes. Having taken many various kinds of precious jewels, he was then about to set sail and return to Jambudvīpa.”
At that time, the sea deity wept aloud with a loud voice, and many dragons harbored anger and desired to harm the merchants.

There was a dragon king named Aśvajit, who was a great bodhisattva born among the dragons due to his original vows; he gave rise to a heart of compassion, rescued and protected the merchants, and enabled them to pass safely across the great ocean to the other shore, after which the dragon king returned to his own dwelling place.

At that time, there was also a great and wicked rākṣasa who followed the merchants like a shadow follows a form, intending to inflict violence and harm; on that very day, this wicked rākṣasa unleashed a great and violent wind.

At that time, the merchants were bewildered and distressed, losing their way; overcome with great terror, they wailed aloud, invoking the various devas—Maheśvara, the Water Deity, the Earth Deity, the Fire Deity, and the Wind Deity—and further calling upon their parents, wives, children, and kinsmen, praying: "May you rescue and deliver us!"
"Good son! At that time, with my pure divine ear, I heard his voice; I immediately went to his side and comforted him with gentle words:
'Do not give rise to fear. I shall show you the way and lead you back to Jambudvīpa in safety.'"
"Good son! At that time, I bound my arms with white cotton cloth, drenched them in oil, and lit them as torches. I then uttered these words of truth:

'In the past, within the Urumuṇḍavana forest, for thirty years I diligently cultivated the four immeasurable minds. For the sake of all sentient beings, I ate only wild fruits and exhorted eighty-four thousand nāgas, yakṣas, spirits, and others, so that they did not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, I now burn this arm to demonstrate the Way, so that these merchants may return safely to Jambudvīpa.
He burned his arm for seven days and seven nights, and these merchants soon returned safely to Jambudvīpa.
“Good son! At that time, I further made this virtuous vow:

‘If Jambudvīpa lacks various precious jewels, and if I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and realize my own benefit, I shall act as a caravan leader and cause seven showers of jewels to rain down upon each and every world.’”
Furthermore, they enter the great ocean to retrieve wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*), and in each and every world-system, they rain down various kinds of miscellaneous precious objects.
In this manner, they proceed sequentially throughout this entire world, and likewise throughout the infinite, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds of the ten directions.

“Good son! All the vows I have made in the past have been fully accomplished. Throughout great kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have constantly acted as the supreme caravan leader; in five-turbid evil worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have rained down various kinds of rare treasures, raining them seven times within a single day. Having thus benefited immeasurable sentient beings and caused them all to become fully satisfied with these rare treasures, I then exhorted and transformed them, establishing them so that they dwell within the Three Vehicles.”

"Good son! You should now know that this is precisely the Tathāgata’s relinquishing of all precious jewels as the causal condition for the roots of goodness through which he attained the various marks."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

After another immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable number of kalpas had passed, this Buddha-world was renamed Jāla (The Net), and the kalpa was named Jñānasampanna (Endowed with Knowledge). That world was characterized by the five turbidities, and the lifespan of its people reached fifty thousand years."
By virtue of his original vow, he was born into a Brahmin family in Jambudvīpa, named Sūgandha. He studied and recited the non-Buddhist scriptures and the *Chāndas* verses.
At that time, sentient beings were largely attached to the view of eternalism; they fought and quarreled with one another, harboring thoughts of enmity and banditry.

At that time, by means of my powerful authority, I taught all sentient beings that the five aggregates of clinging are like enemies, that the twelve sense bases are like an empty village, and that the nature of the twelve links of dependent origination is birth and cessation; I revealed and analyzed *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) and caused them to practice it, further saying:
"O virtuous ones!..."
"Now you may give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, and you should dedicate whatever roots of goodness you have performed.
At that time, I spontaneously attained the five supernatural powers of a rishi.
At that time, there were again immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of people who, by receiving my instruction, all attained the five supernatural powers.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who, having distanced themselves from strife and quarrels and extinguished their enmity and hatred, left the household life to enter the mountains; there they ate fruits and melons, cultivating and accumulating the four immeasurable minds day and night.

When this kalpa was nearing its end, these people dispersed one by one to travel throughout Jambudvīpa to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to leave behind strife and contention, eliminating enmity and hatred, and bringing all to tranquility. Whether there were floods or droughts, violent winds or calamitous rains, they caused them all to cease; the earth became soft and supple, the five grains ripened, and the flavors of food became exquisite.
As the kalpa was nearing its end, sentient beings were once again tormented by various kinds of illness and suffering. "Good son!
At that time, I immediately reflected:
"If I cannot eliminate the illnesses of sentient beings, I shall not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; rather, I shall sever and remove the afflictions for the sake of all sentient beings."
By what means shall I now eliminate the illnesses of sentient beings? There is only one way:

to assemble the entire great multitude—the Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings, as well as the various celestial seers, nāga seers, and human seers—to inquire about medical prescriptions, gather all manner of herbs, and employ various incantations and arts to treat their many ailments.

Having reflected thus, he immediately used his supernatural power to travel to the abodes of Śakra-devendra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, as well as the various devas, nāgas, and ṛṣis, and spoke these words:
"There is Mount Vidyutprabha; I pray that all of you, sirs, assemble together."
At that time, having heard these words, the great assembly gathered together.

Once assembled, they all collectively recited and maintained the Vedic incantations (*vidyā-mantras*); by the power of these, they were able to repel all malevolent spirits and demons, protecting sentient beings. Furthermore, they practiced medical prescriptions, capable of treating phlegm, wind, cold, heat, and fever.
By these causes and conditions, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of people were made to be free from all suffering and affliction. "Good son!
At that time, I further made this vow:

"If I have already acted as the light of wisdom for the immeasurable sentient beings of this one world, establishing them in the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, closing the gates to the three evil realms, opening the path for devas and humans, removing all suffering of illness, and causing them to obtain joy;
and furthermore, I shall successively act as the light of wisdom, even unto joy, for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) persons."
By virtue of the causal conditions and karmic retribution of these roots of goodness, may all my vows be fulfilled and I attain my own benefit.

Just as I have, for the sake of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) beings in this one world-system, closed the gates of the three evil realms and opened the path to gods and humans; and just as I have, for the sake of all those who are ill, invoked the devas, nāgas, and seers to assemble on Mount Vīra and practice the *Vidyā* mantras, thereby causing immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable beings to be entirely freed from illness and receive happiness—so too shall it be throughout this entire Net World, benefiting all immeasurable sentient beings wherever they may be, establishing them in the Three Vehicles, closing the gates of the three evil realms, and opening the path to gods and humans.

Furthermore, for the sake of those who were ill in such worlds, he invited various devas, nāgas, and seers to assemble at Mount Vīra to practice the *Vidyā* mantras, so that immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) beings in these worlds might all be freed from illness and attain happiness.
"As it is with this world, so it is with as many worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; the five turbidities of these evil ages are likewise. "Good son!

At that time, while I was in the Net World, and throughout as many worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—all those evil ages of the five turbidities—I achieved the fulfillment of every vow I had made."

"Good son! You should now know that this is precisely when the Tathāgata, while still a bodhisattva, increased his wisdom and cultivated the bodhisattva path; this is called the Tathāgata’s nurturing of the seeds of the roots of goodness of the three karmas."
The Sutra of the Compassionate Flower, Scroll Nine;
The Sutra of the Compassionate Flower, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Five, Part Three: The Perfection of Giving.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Silent Intent: "Good son!
Thereafter, after the passage of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this world-system changed its name to "Selection of All Evils.
At that time, the great kalpa was named "Equal Canopy of Goodness," and the age was likewise characterized by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
To the east, fifty-four worlds away from here, there is a Jambudvīpa named Luvāra.

By the power of his vows, he was born therein as a Cakravartin King, ruling over the four continents; he was named Ākāśaviśuddha and instructed all sentient beings to dwell securely in the ten wholesome paths of action and within the Three Vehicles.

At that time, I gave everything away without making any distinctions. Then, many immeasurable beggars came and asked me for various kinds of treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, currency, blue lapis lazuli beads, great blue lapis lazuli, and fire-gem *maṇi* jewels. The treasures I possessed were too few to mention, yet the beggars were immeasurable. At that moment, I immediately asked my ministers:
"From where do such treasures originate?"
The minister replied:

"This is what has been manifested by these dragon kings; although such treasures exist, they are intended solely for the service of a noble wheel-turning monarch and cannot be distributed so extensively to beggars such as these."

"At that time, I made this great vow: 'If, in the future, amidst the five turbidities and amidst thick and heavy afflictions when the human lifespan is one hundred years, I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and if my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, I shall become a Great Dragon King and manifest various treasuries of rare jewels. Within these selected evil worlds, throughout every part of the four continents, I shall take birth seven times in each continent. In each of those bodies, I shall manifest immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of treasuries of rare jewels. Each treasury shall be exactly one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, filled with all kinds of rare jewels, to be bestowed upon sentient beings as described above.'"

Just as I have applied myself with diligent effort in this one world, so shall I proceed in succession through all the worlds of the ten directions—those worlds of the five turbidities and evil ages, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, where no Buddha currently dwells—receiving birth seven times in each and every world within each and every Buddha-land, even as previously described.
"Good son! I made such a virtuous vow.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of billions of devas and humans were in the void, raining down various kinds of flowers and praising me, saying:"
"Excellent! Excellent!
You have now attained all forms of giving, just as you have wished in your heart."
"Good son! At that time, when the great assembly heard that King Viśuddhagaganarāja had been given the name 'Sarvadatta' by the devas, they said to one another:
'We should now go and beg for things that are difficult to give away; if we can renounce them, we may truly be called "givers of all."'
"If he is unable to do so, how can he be called one who gives all?
At that time, each of the people individually petitioned the king for his palace ladies, court maids, and children.
When the Wheel-Turning King heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and he granted them everything they requested.
At that time, the people spoke to one another again:
"Such things as wives and children are easy to give away; this is no difficult matter."
"Now I shall beg from the King for his limbs and members; if he can relinquish them, he may truly be called one who can renounce everything.

At that time, the people went to the Great King's presence. Among the crowd was a beggar named Light of Blue Radiance (Candrābhāsa), who observed the "dog precepts," and addressed the Wheel-Turning King with these words:
"Great King, if you are a giver of all things, I pray only that you grant me this Jambudvīpa."

Having heard this, my heart was filled with great joy; I immediately bathed that person with scented water, dressed him in soft and exquisite garments, performed the consecration by pouring water upon his head, and installed him as the successor to the holy throne of the king, bestowing upon him the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
He further made this vow:
"By virtue of this cause and condition of giving away this Jambudvīpa, may I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding the fulfillment of his aspirations and the attainment of his own benefit: all the people throughout Jambudvīpa shall obey, revere, and honor this person as their king.
Furthermore, I shall cause this person’s lifespan to be immeasurable and establish him as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
Once I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall grant him the prediction that he shall attain the state of a Buddha in his very next life.
"Then there was a brahmin named Lu-zhi who came again and begged me for both my feet.
Upon hearing this, joy arose in my heart; I immediately took a sharp blade, severed my two feet myself, and gave them to him as a gift. Having made the offering, I made this vow:
'May I, in a future life, fully attain the unsurpassed feet of precepts.'"
There was a Brahmin named Daṃṣṭra who came again and begged me for my two eyes.
Upon hearing this, joy arose in my heart; I immediately plucked out my two eyes and gave them to him. Having made the gift, I made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, attain the complete and unsurpassed five eyes."
Not long after, there was a brahmin named Śuddhadṛḍha who came once more to beg from me for my two ears.
Upon hearing this, joy arose in my heart; I immediately cut off my own ears and gave them to him. Having given them, I made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, attain the fully perfected ear of unsurpassed wisdom."
Not long after, a Nirgrantha named Saṃjñā came again to beg from me for my male organ.
Upon hearing this, joy arose in my heart; I immediately cut it off myself and gave it to him as a gift. Having given it, I made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and obtain the mark of the horse's organ."
Before long, another person came and begged for my body, flesh, and blood.
Upon hearing this, joy arose in my heart, and I immediately gave it to him. Having given it, I made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, be fully endowed with the unsurpassed mark of golden color."
Not long after, there was a brahmin named Madhurasa who came again to beg for my two hands.
Upon hearing this, joy arose in my heart; taking a knife in my right hand, I immediately severed my left hand and spoke these words:
"Now this right hand cannot cut itself; you may take it yourself."
Having made this offering, he further made a vow, saying:
"May I, in a future life, fully attain the supreme Hand of Faith. "Good son!
After I had severed these various limbs and joints, blood flowed from my body, and I again made this vow:

"By virtue of this giving, may I certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; if my aspiration is fulfilled and I obtain my own benefit, may the remaining parts of my body be received by others once more."
At that time, those who were not noble ones did not understand the meaning of his thoughts, and the various minor kings and great ministers all spoke thus:
"Alas, you foolish man!
Why do you cut off the limbs and members of your own body, causing your sovereign power to perish in an instant? What value is there in these remaining lumps of flesh?"
At that time, the ministers took my body and carried it to a wilderness cemetery outside the city, each returning to their own quarters.
Thereupon, immeasurable numbers of mosquitoes, gadflies, and flies began to suck my blood, while foxes, wolves, jackals, vultures, and eagles all came to devour my flesh.
At that time, while my life had not yet been severed, joy arose in my heart and I made this vow:

"Just as I have relinquished all sovereignty and my limbs and joints, and have not given rise to even a single thought of anger or regret, if my vow is fulfilled and I attain my own benefit, may this body become a great mountain of flesh; may all sentient beings who drink blood and eat flesh come here in their entirety and drink and eat at their will."

Having made this vow, there were immediately sentient beings who all came to devour him; by the power of his original vow, his body grew larger, reaching a height of one thousand yojanas and a width and breadth of exactly five hundred yojanas.
Throughout a full thousand years, I gave this flesh and blood as alms to sentient beings.

During that time, I caused my sacrificed tongue-roots to satisfy all tigers, wolves, owls, crows, eagles, and vultures; yet by the power of my vow, they were restored to their original state. Even if they were gathered together, they would equal Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Having made such offerings, I further made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, fully attain the mark of the broad and long tongue."

“Good son! At that time, when my life in Jambudvīpa had ended, by virtue of my original vow, I was born among the nāgas as a great nāga king named Śrīgarbha-vyūha-darśana (Manifestation of the Treasure Store). On the very night of my birth, I manifested hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of various treasure stores and proclaimed:
‘At this moment, there are many treasure stores here, fully replete with all kinds of rare and extraordinary objects, from gold and silver up to maṇi jewels.’”
When these sentient beings heard this proclamation, each took as many precious objects as they desired and used them as they pleased.
Having done so, they fully practiced the ten paths of wholesome action, gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or gave rise to the minds of *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.

At that time, I was among the dragon kings and took birth seven times; my lifespan lasted for seventy-seven thousand *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of years, during which I manifested immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) treasuries of jewels and gave them to all sentient beings.

At that time, while establishing immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable beings within the three vehicles, he exhorted them to fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action. Having filled sentient beings with various kinds of immeasurable precious jewels, he further made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, be fully endowed with and attain the thirty-two marks of a great man."

"In this same way, on the second continent, he was likewise born seven times as a great dragon king; thus, throughout every single one of the four continents in all places across the entire world-system of Selection, he performed such immeasurable benefits."

Even unto the immeasurable, boundless Buddha-less worlds throughout the ten directions, in each and every world and in each and every realm therein, he likewise underwent seven births as a great Dragon King, with a lifespan of seventy-seven thousand *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of years, manifesting such immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) treasuries in exactly the same manner.

"Good son! You should now know that this refers to when the Tathāgata, while still a bodhisattva, practiced profound and earnest diligence in seeking the causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks."

“Good son! When the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, his practice of diligence surpassed all others; among those of the past, no one else could equal him, with the exception of the aforementioned eight persons.”
If the past did not exist, one should know that future bodhisattvas likewise would be unable to practice such profound and earnest diligence as I have practiced.

“Good son! After the passage of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this world-system will change its name to Coral Pond (*Sāgaraputra*), and the kalpa will be named Flower Hand (*Puṣpahasta*). At that time, there will be no Buddha, and that world will be characterized by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).”

Within that realm, I became Śakra-devānām-indra, named Sunlight of Virtue (Sudarśana-prabhā). Observing Jambudvīpa, I saw that sentient beings were turning toward unwholesome dharmas; I then immediately transformed myself into the likeness of a yakṣa, with a terrifying form, and descended to Jambudvīpa to stand before the people.
When people see me, they all feel fear and ask me: "What do you require?
Please tell us quickly."
I then replied: "I require only food and drink; there is nothing else I need.
The man asked again:
"What do you wish to eat? I replied again,
"I only wish to kill people and devour their flesh and blood."

If you can maintain the precept against killing, up to and including right view, for as long as life lasts, and give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or even the mind of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, I shall no longer devour you.
“Good son! At that time, I constantly manifested as a transformed person to provide food and drink.

When the sentient beings of that time saw me in this way, their fear redoubled; they all, for the remainder of their lives, received the precept against killing, up to and including right view. Some gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, while others gave rise to the minds of *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.
Having exhorted all sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa to practice the ten wholesome paths and abide in the Three Vehicles, I further made this vow:

"If I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and my aspirations are fulfilled so that I may achieve my own benefit, I shall further exhort the people of these four continents to practice the path of the ten wholesome deeds, even until they fill this entire world; in every place throughout the four continents, by means of such manifestations, I shall cause all sentient beings to practice the ten wholesome paths and exhort and transform them to give rise to the mind of the Three Vehicles."

Having thus filled one world-system, it is likewise so throughout the ten directions, in all immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds of the five turbidities and evil ages where there are no Buddha-lands.

"Good son! At that time, having made this vow, I accomplished everything. In the world-system Coral Pond, I manifested as the form of a terrifying yakṣa to subdue sentient beings, causing them to abide in the ten wholesome paths of action and within the three vehicles."

In this manner, throughout the ten directions—in immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds of the five turbidities where there are no Buddha-lands—he manifests in the form of a yakṣa to subdue sentient beings, causing them to practice the ten wholesome deeds and abide within the three vehicles.

In the past, when sentient beings were terrified, I caused them to practice the ten wholesome deeds and abide within the Three Vehicles. By virtue of these karmic causes and conditions, I have now attained the seat beneath the Bodhi tree. As I was about to realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, together with his great assembly, came to where I was, desiring to obstruct and disrupt my path to enlightenment.
“Good son! To speak briefly, when I was a bodhisattva, this was my perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), good son!”

As for the profound dharmakṣānti of the great bodhisattvas, their subtle and wondrous dhāraṇīs, and their liberations and samādhis—I had not yet attained any of these at that time, with the sole exception of my two bodies, my out-flowing five supernatural powers, and my [limited] penetrations.

At that time, I performed this great deed, establishing immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of people in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; establishing immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of people in the vehicle of the *pratyekabuddhas*; and establishing immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of people in the vehicle of the *śrāvakas*. How much more so for those who also obtained the opportunity to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a single Buddha-world—wherein the merit gained from each Buddha is like the number of drops in the waters of the great ocean—and likewise for those who made offerings to immeasurable *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, teachers, parents, and seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
In the past, when I was a bodhisattva, I personally provided my own flesh and blood to sentient beings; such was my great compassion, which none of the arhats today possess.

6. Chapter on Entering the Samādhi-gate of Meditative Concentration. *The Sutra of the Compassionate Flower*, Chapter Six: Entering the Samādhi-gate of Meditative Concentration. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Silent Mind (*Acalamanas*), saying: “Good son!

Just as I now, with the Buddha-eye, see the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the worlds of the ten directions—equal in number to the atoms within a single buddha-field—who have entered parinirvāṇa, all of them were previously exhorted and transformed by me to first resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practice the pāramitās, from dāna-pāramitā up to prajñā-pāramitā; it shall be the same in future ages as well.

“Good son! I now see these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in this eastern world-system, who are currently turning the wheel of the true Dharma; they are also those whom I previously first exhorted to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and to practice the six pāramitās.”
It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. "Good son!

Eighty-nine billion Buddha-worlds away from here to the east, there is a world named Good Flower (*Sukusuma*). In it dwells a Buddha, titled the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Vimalaguṇaprabhāsarāja. He currently resides there, preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
